chapters.title: The Basement
paragraphs: Burgundy had been awake for thirty-one hours.
He could tell by the count blinking in the corner of his monitor, the timer he set to motivate himself. The number didn't bother him. The shake in his right hand did.

It was long past midnight, which made the birthday over. His seventeenth. The feast had run late, the long tables in the great hall taking hours to empty, and he had come down here while the lamps in the upper corridors were still being put out.

In the morning he would walk into the Kings' Hall for the first council of his training. That was what seventeen meant, for a prince of Dross. Nobody had asked him and nobody had needed to: at seventeen a prince presents himself and begins to learn to rule, and for a week the palace had been readying him for that door, the council coat delivered to his rooms, the schedule copied out in a clerk's hand, the same quiet bustle it gave a collection day.
The robot under the tarp was his own idea. Nobody had asked for that either.
Tomorrow morning his father would look at him longer than he had in years. He wanted that look to land on the machine first.
Then him.

The basement smelled like smoking copper. Cables ran along the floor in bundles thicker than his arm, taped down with whatever he'd had on hand: duct tape, electrical tape, in one place a strip of his own shirt. Against the far wall, beneath a tarp, the prototype waited.
He hadn't looked at it in six hours. That was on purpose. If he looked he'd find something to fix, and he didn't have time to fix anything else. Tomorrow was the day.

Three monitors glowed in front of him: torque curve on the left, strain-gauge table in the middle, and on the right a text editor open on a function he had named GO. On the third line from the top there was an off-by-one error he had been looking at for almost an hour without seeing.

He saw it now. He pressed the tab key. He pressed it again. He pressed it a third time and committed the fix and ran the simulation again and watched the torque curve resolve into something less ugly than it had been.
He let out a breath. An eye twitched.

Above him, somewhere, the palace was quiet. The palace was always quiet at this hour. Even the kitchens, which started before dawn, had not yet started. Burgundy could hear the boiler in the next sublevel, a low irregular cough that had been part of the basement's soundtrack for so long that he no longer heard it unless he listened. He listened for a moment. Then he stopped listening and pressed his hands against his eyes and counted to ten.

He knew the kitchens better than a prince was supposed to. When he was small he had spent more hours there than anywhere in the palace, on a stool near the ovens where it was warm, watching Tuck's mother work.
Tuck's family had cooked for the crown for four generations. People said it the same way every time, *four generations*, as though it were a title, and in a way it was.

Tuck's mother was one of the few people his own mother trusted. She raised Burgundy in between her kitchen shift, and sometimes during, placing him on a stool and tearing the heel off a fresh loaf and pressing it into his hands without a word, still hot enough to hurt, and he would eat it standing up, and the smell of it, yeast and iron and woodsmoke.
He was seventeen now and had been working on this thing for two years. His *prototype,* he called it to himself. This project no one knew about. No one but Tuck.

Two years. Or, that was the official count. The truth was he had been working on something like the prototype for nine years, since he was eight years old, when he had taken apart the desk clock in the receiving room and put it back together upside down on purpose to see if his father would notice.

His father had not noticed for two months. When he had noticed, he had cuffed Burgundy on the side of the head and told him to leave the clock alone. Burgundy had taken it apart again that night and put it back the right way, and his father had never mentioned it again.
He thought, sometimes, about the miners. The people the planet ran on.

He did not know any of them. He could not have. He was the prince, and the prince did not go into the mines except to stand at the rim during inspections, in the embroidered coat his father made him wear, while the foremen read from their clipboards and the King nodded at whatever they said.

Once, only once, he had gone below the rim. He was twelve. The inspectors had opened a new corvite vein in the South 12 Shaft and his father wanted it shown to him, so they went down in the cage together, ringed by soldiers, half an hour of dropping through rock before the doors opened. South 12 was the deepest working on the planet. Tunnels forked off tunnels, decades of digging, and no one man alive knew the whole of it.

At the bottom the work lights ran along the walls in a long string, and the air was so thick with dust that the light looked like it was full of something solid. Lines of men were working the rock. Between the men, smaller and quicker, children, sorting and hauling the black crumbs that came off the wall. A smell came up from under everything, sulfur, strong enough to taste at the back of the throat. One of the attendants put a lozenge in Burgundy's hand, honey-colored, sweet, made to kill the smell, and when Burgundy looked at it too long the man tipped the tin and gave him a handful, and Burgundy put them in his coat pocket.

They walked the new vein while a foreman pointed and his father nodded. On the way back to the cage they passed a boy working a chisel into a seam at knee height. He was Burgundy's age, or near it. His hands were grey to the wrist, and the chisel had been ground down to half a chisel. Burgundy took one of the lozenges out of his pocket and put it in the boy's hand.
His father turned, slapped it out of the boy's hand, and crushed it under his heel. He told Burgundy he was not to do that. Then they walked on to the cage, and nothing else was ever said about it.

Five years now. The boy would be seventeen too, or near it. Burgundy did not know his name, or whether he was still on a chisel, or still in South 12 at all. He knew what the crews down there ate, because his tutor had told him once: greycaps, the pale fungus that grew along the walls of the deep mines, cut and dried and boiled into broth. On one visit to the rim a foreman had complained that the men spent their break hours crawling the side tunnels for greycaps instead of resting. That was the whole of what he knew about the boy's life. That, and the smell of the air he worked in.
The thing under the tarp traced back to him. A machine that could take the chisel out of his hands.

He had not told anyone this. He was aware that it was the sort of thing that would sound stupid if he said it out loud, *I built it for a boy whose name I do not know*, and he was aware that this was also possibly true.

And not only his. The prototype was one machine, but the notebooks under the bench held a hundred of them on paper: shaft plans, output tables, arithmetic he had run so many times he could recite it without looking, what the southern seams would give up if the cutting never had to stop and breathe. A third more ore inside a year, tooled properly, at scale. He had run the sum twice, then a third time, because he did not trust the first two.

His father ruled by a craft that had been handed down to him, the same shape passed along five times now, never explained, only inherited. Burgundy had a craft too, he had decided somewhere in the second year, and nobody had handed it to him. It could be measured. It could be proven on a page. When the crown came to him, and it would, the mines of Dross would not run on boys with chisels. That was not a wish. It was a number, and the number had his name on it.
He had not said any of that out loud either.
His father did not know about the basement.
Or, Burgundy hoped his father did not know about the basement. It was possible that he did.
His father was the King of Dross, a small planet that was mostly uninhabitable ice sheet, but that was packed with valuable ores.

"Our ores make travel between the stars possible" is something his father would say at the dinner table at least once a month. Whoever sat at the table heard it: Burgundy, a visiting dignitary, a governor, a minister. Burgundy didn't really understand what it meant. He never asked.
The tribute ships came every month and he had watched them for as long as he could stand at a window. Massive cargo vessels descending onto the planet to collect.

From that same window he could see the city. Kettletown. The planet's capital. It fell away from the castle walls in stacked tiers, houses built on the roofs of houses, iron sheeting gone orange with rust. In the warm months it looked like one great heap of salvage. In the cold months the snow came and settled over all of it and softened the rust to grey.

When he was very small he had asked his father what *tribute* was. What they loaded into the massive vessels. What were they taking away from our planet. *Everything*, his father had said. He didn't explain.

He had learned, eventually, the name of the man whose ships these were. He had never met the man. Nobody on Dross had ever met him. Nicholas was a name his father said the way other people talked about the season's rainfall, as a fact of the world that determined abundance or scarcity. It was all Nicholas.
The basement where he now worked had been a wine cellar once, before some great-great-uncle had decided wine was beneath royal dignity.
The bottles had been carried up and broken in the courtyard to make the point.
He had found the cellar when he was twelve and run the cables down himself, through a vent shaft.

Everything else in here he had scavenged: a motor left to rust in the servants' courtyard behind the kitchens, ball bearings from a broken serving cart, copper wire he stripped from a wall no one had lit in years.
And then he would work. Not *for* anyone. For himself.
He had told himself, sometimes, that he was preparing for something.
He had not been sure, until this year, what.
He ran the arm sequence from the console, the tarp still down. Fluid and smooth. It would be impressive tomorrow.
"Run it again," he said.

The panel brightened. A line of green resolved on the middle monitor, torque holding flat across the curve where last week it had collapsed. The machine gave the small tone it gave when a routine finished clean, one note, low.

"Good prototype," Burgundy said. He had never named it. Tuck's mom named everything: the boiler and the bread knife, her favorite cutting board, gave them all people-names, and Burgundy had decided years ago that naming objects was a way of lying to yourself. So he just said "prototype" to it.
"He's going to hate it," he said. And sighed a long breath.
The panel pulsed, slow, the way it pulsed when it was only waiting.
He had been careful in his rehearsals not to imagine his father laughing.
His mother had given him a glance, at the feast.

That was all. A glance. The birthday feast was the one dinner of the year held at the long tables in the great hall, and his seventeenth had filled them: governors down from the iron country, ministers and their wives in dresses that had crossed systems to reach Dross, the master of the eastern works refilling the King's cup before it was empty. Burgundy sat at his father's right hand and was looked at all evening by people who were actually watching his father.

Late in it, the finance minister stood with his cup and gave the toast everyone had come to hear. Three years to the Vicentennial, he said. Three years, and the prince to his first council in the morning, and the whole long work beginning. The hall drank to it. His father raised his cup at the toast and set it down and did not look at him.

And somewhere in the noise after, his mother looked at him across the table, briefly, and then looked away. An hour later, while a governor was telling the King a long story about grain, she did it again. He had spent his whole life noticing the things she did not say and trying to assemble them, and he had never quite managed it.
He was probably inventing it.

The code terminal blipped. The torque simulation had finished and produced an output graph he stared at for almost a minute before he understood what he was looking at. The graph was fine. The graph had been fine the last three times he had run it. He was running the simulation because he could not think of anything else to do, and he could not think of anything else to do because he was very tired.
He looked at his hand. Still shaking.
He looked at the timer in the corner of the monitor. The number had ticked over to thirty-two hours.
He should sleep. He knew he couldn't.

At the feast, a governor's wife had asked him, kindly, what came next for him, and then answered her own question before he could open his mouth. The training, of course. Then the rite, at twenty. Then the tour of the system. She had counted it off on her fingers. Everyone at that table could have. His whole life, said in one breath, by a woman whose name he never caught.

He was going to be king. That had never been the question. There was no other heir and no other outcome, and he did not lie awake wishing there were. What he lay awake on was the rest of it, the part that could be counted off on a stranger's fingers, a path worn pale before he was born.
The boiler coughed below.
Somewhere far above him, the palace clock struck three.
He laid his head down on his arms.

He told himself it was only for a moment. He told himself he just needed his eyes to stop hurting. He told himself a few more things, small reasonable things, and then, between one of those things and the next, he was no longer telling himself anything at all.

chapters.title: I Rule Men
paragraphs: The Kings' Hall was the most used room in the castle. It was where all the decisions were made, mostly during morning council.

It was not beautiful. The King had spent his money elsewhere: a massive boulevard approaching the palace, rebuilt to be twenty lanes wide and flanked with carved stone giants of Burgundy's ancestors; or the stables, rebuilt twice, stocked with beasts from other systems. There was a private hunting ground, walled and kept and grain-fed the whole year round, so that the King could shoot one morning of it.
The hall did not get any attention. It was long, with an arched ceiling, stone ribs fanning out from the tops of the columns, and was mostly empty. The walls were the same grey stone as the floor.

Down the center of the long hall ran a single pale path, the stone worn a shade lighter by the feet of everyone who had ever walked from the huge entrance doors to the back side of the hall where the throne sat, atop a dais three steps up.

The hall did have one thing worth looking at. Behind the King's throne, a massive window ran nearly floor to ceiling. A thousand small panes of colored glass. And set among them, thin cut sheets of translucent stone, the rare kind pulled from Dross's deepest mines.
In daylight the stone panes would catch the sunlight and split it into gleaming threads of colored light in ways no glass ever could. And at night the stone glowed faint and pale like embers.

The window was the work of one of Burgundy's great-grandfathers, a king who had been obsessed with the stars. He had taken his cosmology from the Ghai, the ancient underground people who had lived here for a thousand years before Burgundy's clan conquered.
He built the window based on their reading of the sky: every pane placed so that the sun, moving through the seasons, would strike certain stones on certain days.

Each alignment meant something. The light on one stone marked the turning of the year; on another, a planting; on another, the harvest. *What harvest?* Burgundy always thought whenever his tutor would try to explain the cosmology of the big window to him pane by pane. He never asked out loud.
He had asked about Nicholas exactly once, when he was ten, in a geography lesson, in the flat bored voice he had already learned to use for the questions that mattered.
"Where does he keep his fleet," he said, not looking up from the star chart. "Nicholas. Between collections. Where do the ships go."
The tutor did not answer for a moment. When Burgundy looked up the man had gone still in a particular way, his stylus lifted off the slate and held there.
"We do not have that on the chart," the tutor said.
"But someone knows."
"Someone knows," the tutor agreed, and set the stylus down, and pulled out a map of the northern fields as though the northern fields were the most urgent thing in nine systems.
And there was no more talk of Nicholas.
On this particular morning, the first morning of his training, Burgundy had not planned to arrive late.

The council coat had come down from his rooms two nights before and hung since on the back of the basement door: heavy wool dyed the clan red, the clan's mark embroidered across the back and both shoulders in thread laid on so thick he could read the pattern with his thumb. He had planned to wake at five, wash, put it on properly, and walk the prototype up the basement stairs with an hour to spare, rehearsing what he would say when his father asked what the machine was. He had not planned to wake at seven, sleeve print on his face, the hours-counter showing thirty-six, his neck stiff in a way he could already tell would last all day.

He rushed to wash his face at the basement basin, and while he washed, the robot booted up across the room. In the thin morning light it looked smaller than it did at night. It stood on its one fat wheel, chest-high, the salvaged frame bolted and rewelded until the seams stood proud of the metal. Two arms, one for grabbing and one for drilling rock. The cutting bit at the drill arm's end was ground down to a dull working shine. Low on the front of the robot was a green-glass panel, where his code lived. This morning the panel pulsed slow and green, and Burgundy looked at the machine whole for the first time since he'd slept and thought, before he could stop himself, that it was either the best thing he had ever made or a toy, and that in a few hours his father would decide which.

The doors of the Kings' Hall had been shut to him at the council hour his whole life. He had walked past them a thousand times. This morning they stood open, because this morning, for the first time, he was expected through them. Nobody knew he was not coming alone.

He came up the last stair in the coat, still settling it across his shoulders, and walked in accompanied by a short robot on a single fat wheel that was proving to be quite loud against the stone. He had not noticed in the basement how loud it was. Down there the ventilation hum had absorbed the sound; up here, on the path of worn stone that ran from the doors to the throne, the wheel sounded like someone dragging a coin across a slate.

The boy and his robot walked toward the throne. His father sat at the far end, flanked by the long dark council tables filled with rows of advisors and stacked paper. The council was on a break. Advisors talked among themselves, their voices an echoing hum in the huge hall.
And behind them, the morning light was blaring through the great glass window, splashing colorful light across the floors and walls of the otherwise grey room.
As Burgundy got closer he caught a clear sight of his father on the throne talking to his security minister.

The King was a large man, broad through the chest, his brow set in a permanent seriousness, his hair going silver at the temples. Around his head he wore a plain band of gold, and set into it, small and unpolished, a strip of each of the eleven minerals the planet gave up.
When Burgundy had been very small he had thought his father was the largest thing in the world. He still thought so sometimes in dreams.

His mother stood beside the throne. Mira's hair was dust-grey, and she wore a gown the color of dried blood. She did not smile when she saw her son. Burgundy felt her watching him, and he searched her face for the look she had given him at the feast the night before. He could not find it. Her council face was on, and nothing in it moved.

As he arrived at the foot of the dais, the group started to go silent and look. The advisors stared, and Burgundy snuck a glance of their confused expressions; the one on the right had a smear of ink on his white collar he did not know was there. The one on the left looked at the prototype briefly and then away.
Burgundy's heart was ramping up.
"Burgundy," the King said, and the hall finished going quiet around the name. "Seventeen." He let the word stand a moment, like a number he wanted the room to look at.
Then his eye went past his son and landed on the machine, and stayed there.
"What is that."

Burgundy stepped forward and so did the robot. The wheel was loud again. Then it parked and lit up, the panel on its chest pulsed green, ready for the demonstration. It made a soft sound, almost like clearing its throat.
"Father," he said. "I want to show you something."
That was not the sentence he had rehearsed. The rehearsed one had numbers in it, and he reached for them now, because the numbers were the part of himself he trusted.

"It cuts rock. I ran it against a test face all year. One of these does the work of two men on a narrow seam, three on a bad one, and it doesn't tire, and it doesn't breathe the air down there. I built it from scrap. The parts cost less than a month of one miner's pay. Tooled properly, at scale, the southern shafts alone would give up a third more ore inside a year. I did the arithmetic twice."
The King looked at the machine longer than Burgundy had expected him to.
"Who taught you this," he said.
"Nobody. I taught myself."
"Nobody," the King repeated, and seemed to put the word away somewhere to be looked at later.
"How many men does one of them replace."
"Two." And, because it was true and he would not be caught rounding a number: "Three, on a narrow seam."
The King was quiet a moment. Then he turned, without any particular hurry, to the tables.

"Gentlemen." He said it easily, the way he said most things to that room. "My son tells me this will bring us a third more ore." He did not look back at Burgundy while he said it. "Perhaps he's right. We are already rich." He let that sit there, unraised, uncontested, and did not wait to see whether anyone smiled.
"It's not only the ore," Burgundy said, before he could stop himself. "It's what we could be, if the shafts ran different, if—"
"If." The King said it once, flatly, and the sentence had nowhere left to go.

He came down the three steps slowly, his coat brushing past the machine's shoulder the way a man brushes past a servant not worth stepping around, and stopped in front of his son, close now, and looked at him instead of it for the first time since he'd entered the hall.

"Ore was never the problem," he said, quieter now, this part not for the room. "There has always been more rock on Dross than men to cut it. Any clerk can count what comes out of the ground. This is where my father started me too." A pause, and Burgundy understood, too late, that it was not a pause for him to fill. "Do you know what it is I rule?"

He had heard the catechism before, somewhere, from someone, and the answer was in him, and it came out smaller than he wanted it to, the way a word had come out of him once at eight years old, holding a clock he had put back together upside down.
"Men."
"Men," the King said. "I rule men."
He let it stand a moment in the quiet hall.

And in the silence Burgundy became aware, all at once, of how much grease was on his hands. It was worked into the creases of his knuckles and under every nail, a night of it, two years of it. He curled his fingers into his palms and slid both fists into the pockets of the coat.

"A foreman walks a narrow seam three times a shift. Not to watch the rock come down. The rock comes down the same whether he's there or not. He walks it because three men working close, hands busy, eyes on the wall, that is when a man says a thing he would never say standing still. Who's short on his rent. Who's angry at his shift boss. Who's been asking questions he oughtn't." He looked past his son, at the machine, and then back. "You've built something that digs quietly and tells me nothing at all. I don't want quiet, Burgundy. I want to know."

"This planet has never been invaded," he said. "Not in five generations. Not because of the ore." He held his son's eyes, and there was nothing of anger in his face at all, only the flat certainty of a man repeating a thing he had said many times, each time as if for the first time to whoever was listening. "Because I know what is moving under it before it moves."
Nobody in the hall stirred.

Then he set his boot against the machine's wheel and pushed, not hard, the way a man tests a cart's brake with his foot, to see whether it holds. The prototype rocked back on its wheel, the green panel flickering once, and somewhere along the right side of the hall one of the advisors made a small, soft sound that might have been a cough and might not have been.
Burgundy heard it.

In the basement, in the long hours of the night, he had run every scenario he could imagine for how this conversation might go. He had imagined the yes. He had imagined the no. He had been careful, he remembered now being careful, not to imagine a laugh. He had not been able to bring himself to imagine a laugh.
But the sound had not come from his father.
It had come from an old man with ink on his collar, an old man whose name Burgundy was not sure he had ever known, an old man who had been standing in this room since before Burgundy was born.
"Take it away," the King said.
"Father—"
"I said take it away."
Then he turned from his son to the tables, and his voice opened out into the one he used for proclamations.
"Gentlemen. My son begins his training today."
He was looking at Burgundy while he said it, and he went on looking at him, and spoke to the room.

"For the next three years he will be schooled in the craft of ruling, as I was schooled, and my father, and his, in the tradition of the clan that has held this planet for five generations. When the training is done, on his twentieth birthday, at his Vicentennial, he will be crowned prince and heir in this hall, before all of you. And he will go out on the tour of the system, as every heir of this line has gone."
He stood over the machine without looking at it.

"The craft of ruling Dross is not a small craft. It asks for discipline. It asks for focus." And then, only then, back to his son, the proclamation dropping away and something flatter underneath it: "You will be here tomorrow morning. Without your toys. Ready to do what it takes to become the king of this place. We will call that the beginning."
Burgundy looked down at the prototype.
"Yes, sir," he said.
He did not look at Mira.
He did not look at the advisors.

He turned the prototype around, by hand, because he did not trust himself to give it a command in a voice that would not crack, and he pushed it back toward the doors. The wheel loud again as it moved across twenty colorful shades of sunlight. The hall behind him silent. Burgundy walked the length of the hall with his hands on the prototype's housing, and at the doors he did not stop, and he did not look back, and he pushed through into the corridor.
The doors closed behind him.
He stood for a moment with his hand on the prototype, in the long cold corridor where his footsteps would have echoed if he had taken any. He stood very still. His right hand was shaking again.
The prototype hummed beside him. Its green panel pulsed once, gently.

chapters.title: Mira's Wing
paragraphs: Through the closed doors, the council resumed. His father's voice was a low rumble without shape. An advisor answered. Then his father again, longer, and something in it must have been a joke, because it got its soft, polite laughs.
He was still listening when the small side door in the corridor  opened.
His mother slipped out.

She did not look at him. She closed the door behind her without a sound. She stood for a moment with her hand still on the handle, listening to the council, until the King said something else that was answered by the same polite noise, and then she turned to Burgundy, and she put one finger against her lips.
"Come," she whispered. It was less a word than a breath. "Bring it." Her eyes went to the robot.
Burgundy opened his mouth.
She shook her head, a single small motion, and turned, and began to walk down the corridor.
He put his hand on the prototype's housing. He pressed the small command that told it to follow. The prototype rolled after him.
They walked.

They took a corridor Burgundy knew, the long one that led past the council chamber toward the eastern courtyards. Then Mira turned right, into a smaller corridor that Burgundy had only walked twice in his life. And from here he began to lose his bearings.
She took him past a door he had believed was a broom closet. Behind the door was a narrow flight of stairs going up.
She started up them without hesitation.

Burgundy stopped at the foot of them. The prototype stopped behind him. Its wheel, a single fat wheel, salvaged from a serving cart, rated for stone floors and stone floors only, was going to have to climb stairs.
He had prepared for this, sort of.

Two months ago, in the basement, he had cut the wheel open. He had lined the inner rim with a rubber sleeve. He then wired a small air compressor into the chest cavity. He had coded a 'soft-mode' that would let the tire release air, enough for the wheel to deform around the edges of steps so it could climb them.

It had worked decently this morning as he took the robot up a few small sets of stairs from the basement to the council. But he had never taken it up a full spiral flight. He had not been sure he would ever need to.
He pressed the command.

The prototype's chest made a small hydraulic sound. The wheel visibly relaxed. It looked, for a moment, as though it had lost some air. Then Burgundy pushed it against the first step. The wheel deformed. It caught. He pushed. The prototype rocked forward, awkward like it was about to fall, but then it mounted the first step, and then the second, and then a rhythm settled into it that was almost a walk. It was climbing.
Mira was five steps up, watching.
"You really built this?" she asked quietly..
"Yes."
She nodded once and kept climbing.
Then, three steps further up, without turning:
"How long."
"Two years."

The stone at the top of the stairs was a different color, warmer, cream instead of grey, and the sconces along the walls were made of a metal he could not immediately identify, worked with a repeating pattern that looked, when he looked closely, like nothing he had seen anywhere else in the palace.  The air smelled different too. Not the wet-stone smell of the palace's lower halls. It smelled like books.
Mira did not stop to let him look.

She took him through a small entry hall, and into a larger corridor with a high vaulted ceiling and windows on one side, all shuttered, all dusty. Their shoes made no sound; the floor here was carpeted, a long red runner going grey. Burgundy realized, walking down it, that the runner had hardly been walked on at all. It felt brand new.
"Mother, where —"
"Not yet."
They passed doors. Most were closed. One was open a crack, and through it Burgundy caught a glimpse of a sitting room, chairs still angled toward each other, but otherwise empty and gathering dust.
They turned a corner. They turned another.
Mira stopped at a set of double doors, pushed them open, and stepped through into a room that stopped him where he stood.

Burgundy had known there was a library in the palace. There were several. The one near the entrance, where his father sometimes met with foreign envoys, had a wall of leather-bound treaties and a globe that had not been updated in his lifetime. The one off the council chamber held the ledgers and the tax records and the tribute receipts. Neither of them was this.
This library was three stories tall and another two stories down, dug deep into the ground, all contained in this one massive room.

The room was cut up into a labyrinth of bookcases and crossings, stacks running into stacks, with narrow iron walkways bridging the gaps at each level so a person could walk from one wall of books to another without ever touching the floor.  There were ladders on brass rails that traveled the length of each wall.
And doors. Dozens of them, small and arched, set into the shelving in no order Burgundy could find. One was half his height. Another only reachable from the iron walkway above.

A spiral staircase in the center connected the whole thing. Down at the basement level stood the tables. Long, dark, oiled, scattered with reading lamps and stacked books, and on one of them a small model of a star system Burgundy did not recognize. A whole corner had been given over to maps and globes.
Tens of thousands of books rose around him, more than he could take in at a glance; on the shelf to his left, close enough to read the spines, half of them were in languages he had never been taught.
He stopped.
The prototype rolled up beside him and stopped too, its wheel humming back to solid mode, its soft-mode air-cycle finishing with a small sigh.
Mira let him look for a moment. Then he asked, "Mother, what is this place?"
She said, without turning:
"This is my library. This whole wing is mine, built at my request when I agreed to marry your father. My mother sent most of these books. This is a piece of my family."
"Your family," Burgundy said.
She turned.
For the first time since the corridor she smiled, a small, thin smile.
"Yes," she said. "My family."

She crossed to a shelf on the eastern wall and climbed the ladder without hurry, and Burgundy followed her up because he did not know what else to do, and the robot waited below on its wheel, its green panel pulsing slowly in the low light. At the top of the ladder Mira walked along the gallery to a specific shelf and stopped in front of it.
The books on the shelf were mostly grey and brown. A few had gold lettering.
One was yellow.
She reached up and put her hand on the yellow book, a plain yellow, no title on the spine, and she looked at Burgundy.
"This," she said, "was your grandfather's."
Then she pulled.

The book came out an inch, then stopped. Something inside the shelf clicked, a small mechanical sound, quiet but precise, and the whole bookcase shifted on some hidden hinge and began to swing inward, silently, like a great door on very old bearings.
Behind the bookcase was another room.

chapters.title: The White Room
paragraphs: The room behind the bookcase was white.

Not painted white. Grown that way, it seemed, the walls paneled in some smooth pale material that was not stone and not wood and not metal exactly. Overhead, no oil lamps, no hanging bulbs. A row of long flat panels shed a clean cold light Burgundy had seen in only one place before.

When he was young, Mira used to take him to watch the royal engineers draft the planet's mining machinery. He would sit for hours if she let him, watching the men bend over their tables with rulers and stacks of paper nearly as tall as he was, all of it lit by the same long flat panels, the same cold clean light.
This room had that light. That feeling. Even the same smell.

The tables ran in rows, like desks, each with its own stool and its own lamp, enough of them for twenty students. On the walls, pinned flat and squared, hung charts and diagrams: the cutaway of an osmarine drive he had never seen the like of, a table of the elements in Core-world lettering, the paths of Dross's two moons drawn out to the one week a year they crossed. At the far end stood a slate board, wiped clean, a tray of chalk beneath it. The chalk was unworn.

The tables themselves were laid out with real equipment. Not scrap. Not salvage. Sealed processors still in their original packaging, manufacturer's marks unbroken on the boxes. Oscilloscopes newer than anything the palace had bought in his lifetime. A small array of green-glass panels stacked between wooden dividers. Toolboxes with drawers labeled in a fine hand he recognized, after a moment, as his mother's. And on the bench nearest the door, laid out in a straight line, a replacement for every part he had ever scavenged: a new motor where his had rusted, bearings finer than any serving cart ever carried, a spool of wire that had never once been inside a wall.

Against the back wall stood a low shelf of documents: folders, ledgers, thin bound reports, all with the same neat spine tags. A stack of manifests. A stack of star charts. A stack of what looked, from where he stood, like schematics.
"Come in," she said.

He walked to the first table and picked up a processor. Turned it over. It was a model he had read about in a manual two years old and never once expected to hold. This single unit was worth more than a year of a miner's pay. There were twelve of them on this table alone.
He set it down. His hand was shaking again, and not from tiredness this time.
"Mother," he said. "What is this room?"

Mira crossed to a chair near one of the tables and sat, straight-backed, hands folded, the way she sat at council. But her face was not the council face. For the first time he could remember, she looked like a person and not a queen.
"Your father does not know about this room, and it must stay that way," she said. "That is the first thing to understand."
"All right."
"No one in your father's line has ever known about it, or about the other rooms I keep in this wing. These are known only to my family."
"Your family?"
She looked at him a moment before she answered.
"Sit down," she said.
He sat.
"You know that I was not from here. You know your father married me as part of a bargain between families. But the version you have been told leaves things out."
"What does it leave out?"
She considered the question.

"My family is not a family the way your father's is. There is no title. No throne. No country. There is a network, very old, very large, spread across nine systems that I know of, and likely more. It moves things. Some of what it moves is legal in some places. Most of it is not legal anywhere. And a great deal of what has kept it in business for two centuries is minerals, the kind that come from inside this planet and nowhere else in this part of the galaxy. The kind that fuel technology like the processor in your hand."
Burgundy looked down. He had picked the processor back up without meaning to.

"Dross means nothing to the Core-world Alliance. Too far, too small. But Dross means a great deal to my family. We move a large share of what this planet produces, not through the tribute channels, those are Nicholas's, he takes the greater part and has for decades. My family takes what's left. Moves it, sells it to whoever will buy, and asks very few questions about what it's bought for."
She paused.

"There has been informal trade between Dross and my people for years. It was never an easy trade. There was mistrust. Now and again, worse than mistrust, because my people are not only traders. They raid as well."
"Raid?"
"They find ships carrying cargo in the remote parts of a system, and they take them. For ransom, sometimes. Sometimes they simply take the cargo and sell it."
"So they're pirates," Burgundy said.

"You could call it that." He could tell she did not care for the word. She went on before he could ask her why. "Your father's father wanted the trade formalized. A treaty, not an understanding. And the marriage was how it was formalized. The marriage was me."
He could not think of anything to say to that.

"I was seventeen," Mira said. "I hadn't much choice in it. I was young, and I had been promised the Core academies since I was a girl, and instead my father called me into his office one afternoon and told me I was going to Dross. That I was to be its new queen. It wasn't customary, we're not royalty, whatever the word means to you, but your grandfather sensed a conflict coming if the families didn't lock themselves together, and my father priced the lock very well. Protection for our ships in three systems. Standing trade with Dross for a generation." She looked at her folded hands and straightened them, though there was nothing to straighten. "That was the deal that was made. I protested. It changed nothing. So instead I asked for the library, a whole wing, and I asked that it be big, and grand. I had dreams, then, of an academy of my own here. Something to modernize this place. My family agreed to fund the wing. Your father's family agreed to build it."
Seventeen.
She had been exactly the age he was now. Three years from tonight, his own tour would be waiting, and somewhere out on it, a stranger who would be brought home to Dross the way his mother had been.
"And the academy?" he asked.

"Your father would never allow it. I did not know that in the beginning. I was hopeful. Naive, if you like. He let me keep the wing, the books, the studies, so long as they stayed mine alone. He put a stop to the rest before it could ever start."

Silence. Her face sat half in the room's cold light and half in shadow. Something rose in his chest that wanted to be let out, to cross the room and lean on her the way he hadn't in years. He held it where he always held it, and it passed, and underneath it he found himself wishing, absurdly, that she would be the one to cry instead.
"How does Father not know about any of this?" he asked instead.
"He believes that what I do in this wing is read books. He has not set foot past that bookcase since three weeks into our marriage. He has never opened this door." She paused. "He is not curious."
She said the word *curious* the way another woman might have said a private endearment.
"Why?" Burgundy said. "Why buy all of this? Why any of it?"

"Because I am curious. I have always been. My grandfather lived through the invention of interstellar travel, and when I was a girl he used to tell me what it did: whole systems pulled out of poverty inside a generation, the moment they could trade across the stars." She held his eyes. "So I have spent nineteen years collecting, and seeding, quietly, into this planet. A disc slipped into a servant's basket. A better pump sent down to a village that had been hauling its water by hand for three hundred years. Small things, for a long time, without a name on any of it." She looked at him. "The people of this planet believe they are poor because the galaxy made them poor. They do not know they have been cut off from it on purpose."
He did not have an answer for that either.
"I decided a month ago that I would show you this room," she said. "I have been watching you, in the basement, for longer than that."
"You know about the basement?"
"I have known about the basement for more than a year. I said nothing. I wanted to see how far you would take it on your own."
He said nothing now either.
"You brought it to him today. Your robot. I knew you would, and I guessed what he'd do with it. I told myself that if he rejected it, it would be time to show you this."
She rose, crossed to a table, lifted a spool of fine-gauge wire, turned it once in her fingers, and set it back exactly where it had sat.
"I am going to offer you a bargain," she said. "I am going to offer it once."
"All right."

"This room is yours. Everything in it. Whatever else you need, name it, and I will find it, even off the Core worlds, the newest discs, and a fair number of parts besides. You will not sneak scrap out of a southern shaft again. You will build here, with real materials, and you will build whatever you want to build."
She looked at him.
"In exchange, you will be the prince your father wants."
He waited.

"You will show up to council every morning. You will wear the coat. You will listen. You will stand at his shoulder at the mine inspections and nod when he speaks and smile the way he wants you to smile. You will be seen at the tribute counts and the seasonal meetings with the regional governors. You will ride to the docks with him each month to watch the shipment loaded. In every public detail, you will be the son he wanted." She paused. "The Vicentennial is three years out, and from now until it comes, everything you do will be measured against that day. He will want the heir polished for it more than he has ever wanted anything from you. Give him that son, and he will not look past him."
"He'll never believe it," Burgundy said.

"He will. He will believe it because he wants to. That is the thing about your father you have not learned yet. He does not see what is in front of him. He sees what he expects to see. Give him exactly that, and he will not look further. He will believe the lecture he gave you today did its work. That you finally grew into the son he always knew you'd be."
Burgundy sat with his hands in his lap and looked at his mother, not at the processors on the table.
"You're asking me to become him," he said.
"I am asking you to *look* like him. Only to keep his eyes off what you are doing here."
"And if he finds it anyway?"
She did not answer right away. Her eyes went once to the bookcase door and came back.

"If your father opens that door, he will not see a library. He will see nineteen years of my family's cargo inside his walls, smuggled past his own customs, under his own roof, on my signature, since the year he married me. There is a treaty underneath this marriage, Burgundy, and this room breaks it, and that treaty is the only thing that has kept his family's ships and my family's ships pointed away from each other for nineteen years. He would seal this wing to the last door. He would send me back. Or I would board one of his ships for home, and the ship would not make port. It is a long crossing." She stopped, and made her hands go still. "What he would do with you, I cannot tell you, because I don't know, and I have thought about it more than I want you to know. It frightens me. Now you've heard me say so, and you will not hear me say it again."
"Do we have a bargain?" she said.
He thought about it.

He thought about his father's boot against the prototype. He thought about the small sound the minister with ink on his collar had made, that might have been a laugh. He thought about the boy in the South 12 Shaft, hands grey to the wrist, working a chisel ground down to half a chisel. He thought about the tribute ships coming down each month, and his father, saying *I rule men.*
"Yes," he said. "We have a bargain."

They stood a moment in the cold light. So much fell into place at once: the stories she had told him as a boy about inventors and star-spanning gadgets, the errands to watch the royal engineer, the tools that turned up on his shelf as if they'd always been there.

She crossed the room and lifted something from the far table, small enough that he couldn't make it out until she pressed it into his hand: a tiny processor unit, newer and finer than the first, fine gold lines worked across its face.
"Begin," she said.

chapters.title: Twilight Freeze
paragraphs: The beginning, the next morning, turned out to be an hour in the great hall: a schedule read out, tutors named, his father gone to the mines before the reading was done. After, the palace went slow and half empty, and Burgundy went back to his mother's wing in the middle of the morning, but he did not go to the white room behind the bookcase. He walked her library instead, the long deep room, morning light streaming in, illuminating the dust in the massive space. He pulled books down at random and put them back, digesting everything that had happened in the last twenty-four hours. None of it would sit still in his mind.

He woke with his head already full. He dressed and went down. Bread, preserved fruit, a cup of the bitter morning tea, his father was already gone to the mines. The beginning, the next morning, turned out to be an hour in the great hall: a schedule read out, tutors named. After, the palace went slow and half empty, and Burgundy went back to his mother's wing in the middle of the morning, but he did not go to the white room behind the bookcase. He walked her library instead, the long deep room, morning light streaming in, illuminating the dust in the massive space. He pulled books down at random and put them back, digesting everything that had happened in the last twenty-four hours. None of it would sit still in his mind.

He climbed down a brass ladder to the bottom of the library and walked to the long dark table strewn with maps. One in particular caught his eye. It showed the palace in fine ink at the center, and around it and below it, spilling down the steep slope in ten thousand small squares, the city. Kettletown. The capital and the largest city on the planet.

He stood in front of it a long time. Another map showed the whole planet. Mostly white. Only a band across the middle was livable, a third of the world, maybe less: the palace, the mines, the three main cities. The rest was ice, and had always been ice. Under the ice, the tutors had taught him, lay more corvite than the whole band would give up in a thousand years, locked beneath ice sheets thicker than the palace was tall. Nobody went out there.
He looked at the streets of Kettletown, the crooked ones that ran down from the wall. He saw one straight street and a label "Bottom Market." And he remembered.
It had started with Tuck. It always did. They were fifteen.
Tuck was the only person alive who knew Burgundy's face and did not call him prince.
Fifteen was the first time Tuck took Burgundy over the wall, into the city.
It was during the Freeze one year.

For most of a hundred days the sun did not clear the hills. It came up to the lip of them and stopped, a low burning orb. It would give eight or nine hours of a red-orange light that threw no shadows, and then it slid back down the way it had come.
The snow would come in batches of big, slow flakes. And it would stay, covering the rusted roofs of the city below the palace and turning the whole slope white and soft and quiet.

During the Freeze the palace turned into a glowing temple of light and heat, smoke rising out of a hundred chimneys. The boilers in the sublevels running non stop day and night.  The windows were double thick, and a boy could live an entire Freeze inside it and never once feel the cold on his skin. Burgundy hated this. He hated the way the palace sealed itself. It made him feel cooped up from a very young age.
In the schoolroom his tutors called it the Twilight Freeze,  they gave three weeks off in the middle of it, during the festival season, and that's when Burgundy would sneak out.
In the schoolroom his tutors called it the Twilight Freeze. They gave three weeks off in the middle of it, during the festival season, and that's when Burgundy would sneak out.

They had been born on the same day, Burgundy and Tuck, in the week the moons locked. The two moons of Dross kept their stations most of the year, the Violet high and small, the Bruise low and red, and month by month they drifted toward each other by degrees too slow to watch, until in the middle of the Steam they came together and locked, the Violet riding onto the Bruise, the red rimming the violet in a ring. They held like that for one week and then let go. On those nights the two lights mixed, and the steam coming off the wet lanes went faintly violet, and no one needed a lantern to walk anywhere. People called the week Twinrise. Princes of the line were always born inside it; that was arranged, like everything about a prince was arranged. Tuck just happened. Tuck's mother told it every year at both their birthdays, which were one birthday, always held in a little room off the kitchens, a rare mix of servant and royal, until the year the boys turned ten.

She had gone into labor in the kitchens with a full tray in her hands, the same night the Queen went into labor upstairs. "The two of 'em," she'd say, beaming, "same night, same cry they both had, the only difference is I still had to get the bread done on time." That was her first punch line.

And then, "Beat the queen to it too. Beat her clean. Tuck popped out two hours before Burgundy. Then I had a cry, had a wash, and was back on the line before the noon rush the next day." Everyone would laugh, and now she was on a roll: "Her Highness up there had the whole floor running round like headless hens and I'm down here going, what's all the fuss?" She'd wink at Burgundy when she got to that part.

And Mira would laugh. She would sit on a kitchen stool in that little room with her hands loose in her lap, and she laughed at Tuck's mother's story in a way Burgundy never heard her laugh anywhere else.

It was Tuck's mother who started the tradition, back when the boys were small enough that she still dressed them both. Each birthday, each boy cut a square from something of his own, a hand-sized square of whatever he had worn through that year, and gave it to the other. The squares went to Tuck's great-aunt Essa, his mother's aunt, a seamstress, who sewed the first years of them into two quilts, one for each bed. After she was gone, Tuck's mother kept the quilts growing. The quilt on Burgundy's bed grew in burlap and kitchen cotton, patched twill, cloth gone soft with boiling. The one on Tuck's grew in fine grey linen and silk.

The parties stopped. The squares did not. A square a year, handed over in a corridor in the two minutes they had, or passed through Tuck's mother, or once slid flat under a door. Neither of them had ever said a word about keeping it going, and neither of them stopped.
At the foot of Burgundy's bed, folded down every night by a servant who had never once asked about it, lay a quilt made of another boy's clothes.

Tuck's great-great-grandmother had been the head cook for the King's great-great-grandfather. They were the rare kind of servant a royal family stops seeing as *just* a servant, and Mira, who trusted almost no one, trusted them.

When Burgundy was small it was Tuck's mother who fed him, who wiped his face, who carried him on her hip through the kitchen steam while his own mother mostly sat behind a closed door in a wing he was not allowed into. The kitchen smelled of yeast and iron and woodsmoke.
Tuck and Burgundy were raised together like brothers. But only to a point.

At six, Burgundy's time came to go to school with the other children of the elite: the security minister's twins, the daughter of the man who governed the western mines, a boy whose father managed the shipping facilities.

They learned figures and the star charts and the history of the clan, while around the same time Tuck went to work. He started in the kitchens the way his mother had, hauling and scrubbing before he was tall enough to reach the counters.

After that, Burgundy saw him in the halls, and that was all. He would come out of the schoolroom in the afternoon and there would be Tuck going the other way with a sack of tubers over his shoulder, his knuckles red from the cold storage.

They would stop. They would talk for a minute, two minutes. Tuck always had something: a rat the size of a cat down in the flour room, a cousin who had lost a finger and kept it in a jar. Then someone would call for one of them, a tutor for Burgundy or *the water is boiling *for Tuck, and they would go their separate ways down the same hall, and Burgundy would carry those two minutes around with him for the rest of the day.
He wanted more of it. He understood, even then, that there was no more of it to be had. One of them wore a coat with the clan's mark stitched at the collar and one of them carried the potatoes.
They found each other again the night Burgundy tried to saw off a wheel.

Burgundy was fifteen and it was the three-week break during the Freeze, and he had been building in the basement for a year. A mechanical arm that could almost pick things up. He wanted to put a wheel on it to see if he could make it balance. He had near stripped the palace of every loose motor and bearing he could carry down the vent shaft. But surely he could find a spare wheel somewhere.

He soon found himself crouched in the corridor near the cold storage one evening, slowly sawing a wheel with a thick rubber tire off a serving cart without anyone noticing, when Tuck came around the corner carrying crates of eggs. Tuck looked at him mid-saw-on-a-cart's-leg. Burgundy popped up and hid the saw and Tuck's face changed.
"So *you're* the ghost," Tuck said.
"What?"

"Cooks been going on about it for a year. Stuff gone missing. A spring suddenly disappears from the potato scale. The little brass gear out of the coffee grinder, the good one, just gone." He grinned. "Nothing worth taking. And that's what's got'em spooked, how it just disappears." He looked at Burgundy's saw. "So it's you."
Burgundy said nothing. His pulse was going.

"Relax." Tuck shifted the crates. "I'm not telling no one. Who would I tell?" he said, laughing. And that was true. And for a moment and all at once, Burgundy felt something in his chest loosen. Something that had been held tight so long he'd forgotten it could.
It was the oldest feeling he had. Tuck on his side, the two of them against whatever it was that day. That was his everyday, until slowly, then quickly, it wasn't.

So he told him. It was the first time he had told anyone. He had been secretly building things in that old wine cellar, currently working on an arm. A motor bolted to a joint that could lift a brick off the bench and set it down again, most of the time. His father would be furious if he found out.  And the next version needed parts the palace did not have.
"Oh, Ran would have a million of those," Tuck said.
"Ran?"
"Ran. My uncle. He runs a salvage yard in town, I'll take you."
And Burgundy, who had never once been outside the wall, said yes before he had finished thinking about it.

chapters.title: Umberroots
paragraphs: The kitchens took deliveries from the city, and the servants had a gate on the low east side, wide enough for a cart, watched by a man who owed Tuck's mother for a Freeze full of hot meals and found a reason to look at the sky whenever the two of them passed.
"Dontchu talk to anyone," Tuck said, the first time and every time after. "You say your words all perfect like you do and you'll give yourself away. Let me talk. You point."
"I will not talk."

"See there you go already *'I will not talk'" *he said in a mocking voice as walked quickly down a servants tunnel that led to the back gate. "Nobody down there has ever said *I will not*. Come on, ghost."

Tuck led the way out the gate, past the guard, and down a path that soon left the palace ground behind and dropped toward the city. The clean stone gave way to packed snow and then to a road of frozen mud.
Ahead, the ground pitched down, and Kettletown came up to meet them, roof below roof below roof, stitched down the whole slope in tin and brick and smoke, the way it had looked from the map.
Houses stood on houses, tin on brick on tin, no plan under any of it, each one leaning on the one below until roofs doubled as the floors of the street above.
Wires ran everywhere, looped wall to wall over the lanes, sagging under caps of snow, spliced and re-spliced at every junction until no one could have said where the power first came from.

Meltwater ran down the wires and froze again into long teeth of ice that Tuck steered him around without looking. Smoke stood up from a thousand stovepipes and went almost nowhere, because in the freeze the air scarecly moved.
A thousand tiny houses with their faint warm light. Pinpricks of orange dotting the landscape of a ten thousand illuminated doorways and windows.
"Welcome to my beautiful city, Ghost" Tuck said, self depricating, half proud. And Burgundy was realizing *Ghost *was becoming his official nickname within their newly rekindled friendship.

They descended flights of uneven concrete stairs serpentining through make shift alleys. And then it came up out of the dusk before he could see the source of it: A smell wafting from somewhere below.

Char, and a spice he had no name for, something dark and warm and faintly sweet that caught in the back of his throat. Then woodsmoke. Then the green raw smell of cut roots. Then a sourness, fermentation, a crock somewhere.
One smell laid over the next, thicker with every step, until they came out of the stacked lanes onto the flat ground at the bottom of the slope and Burgundy saw where it all came from.
"Welcome to the Bottom" Tuck said. "Never thought I'd be taking you here Ghost. This is kinda crazy, keep that coat pulled up around your face."

The Bottom Market ran along a straight road.. The buying and selling took place under a roof of stitched tarp. It was a hundred fires, in a hundred little stalls, and a flurry of dense action that seemed to radiate up off the straight road.

Steam stood up off every fire and stall and hung in the still cold air, a low golden fog lit from beneath by the stove-mouths, and the pale unmoving sun came in sideways under the tarp and turned the steam the color of  honey.
People moved through it close and loud. They were dressed in everything the city had, layered and patched and belted twice against the cold.

They walked past a stall of women cooking around a huge deep pan over coal fire, cutting root vegetables and peppers  and frying them with noodles.  One of the women laughed as she peeled a red potato.

The deeper into the market they went, the denser the crowd. It made Burgundy nervous, being around all these people, but his nerves were overridden with fascination. There was an entire world happening here, a 20 minute walk from the palace, and he had never known about it.
They kept descending deeper into the stream of people and fragrance.
It was the dinner hour. In every stall, stumps for seats and hands wrapped around warm bowls and tins, breath and steam going up together into the golden light.
Tuck was a stall ahead, haggling over something, and for a moment Burgundy stood alone at a pepper seller's table, a woman with a scale and a hundred baskets, and she took him for a customer.
"Go on," she said. "The long red ones. You won't get these up north, not fresh."

He should have pointed. He knew he should have pointed. But she was holding a pepper out to him and asking him a question, and the answer came up out of him in the voice he was born with, before he could stop it, every word of it square and set down in a row.
"Go on," she said. "Taste this one, fresh in this morning, only gunna get worse from here.
He should have pointed. Or walked away.  But she was holding a pepper out to him and asking him to try it, and the answer came up out of him in the voice he was born with,
"Thank you, no. I only wanted to look at them."
It was nothing. It was a polite sentence. Her hand did not stop, but her eyes came up off the scale, the way you look at a coin that rang wrong.
It was nothing. It was a polite sentence. Her hand did not stop. Her eyes did. They came up off the scale and held on him a moment too long.

Then Tuck was there, loud, pulling Burgundy. "Don' mind him, aunt Leel, he's a bit soft, they dropped him on his head when he was small. C'mon, you." He steered him off hard and did not take the arm away until they were three stalls gone, and the arm was tighter than the grin. "What did I tell you. What did I tell you. No talking. This is serious stuff. Don't mess this up."
Burgundy did not answer. His heart was going. But slowly, as they walked, he went back to taking it all in.
He had always thought the low city would be starving.  he had been wrong.

The stalls were heaped with food he could not account for. Roots, mostly, but roots such as never came to his father's table: a deep bruised purple, almost black, cut open to a violet flesh veined in white; a knuckled yellow tuber the length of his forearm; small round ones, red as coals, sold still clumped with the pale soil they came out of.

And peppers in more variety than he could count. Some hung in ropes from the tarp-poles, dried and fresh both. Some peppers were no bigger than his thumbnail and some long and wrinkled and the color of old blood. He saw one stall cutting a big red fresh pepper, the seeds ripped out, the flesh thrown over an open flame so that the spicy smell of them scorching was half of what hung in the air.

There were pale mounds of the greycaps, the mine fungus he did know. Here they were heaped in baskets in a stall selling 100 type of vegetable. There were greens he did not know a frozen planet could grow.

A woman near him was frying a medly of different colored root strips. She cut them on the bias into thin ovals and dropped the long medallions into a pool of bubbling oil and they went from violet to something deeper as they cooked, the edges lacing black and crisp.

And she turned them with two fingers, the same two fingers she then used to grab a thick pinch of a deep red spice powder that she flicked onto the strips followed by a palm-ful of salt she sprinkled with the same twofingers.
And she was talking the whole time to the man who had ordered them, a long complaint about her son in a slang he almost didn't understand.

She laughed at the end of it, scooping the finished medallions of fried root our with a long perforated spoon, into a twist of waxed paper and dashing  more of a different red powder onto the finished product, this one darker. Then on with a generous dollop of a cool green yogurt flecked with herbs.  She handed it across to the man.

The man took it and dropped two coins on her cutting board, saying something back about her son. She burst out laughing and swatted him away without looking, and the steam went up off the oil into the golden light, and Burgundy stood there in his borrowed coat and could not stop looking.
"Oi. Ghost." Tuck pushed the back of his shoulder. "what are you staring at, man. It's a potato, Come on. you want one?" Tuck didnt wait for an answer.

"We'll take an order of hot umberroots just like that" Tuck said, his eyes following the man as he walked off.  The stall woman nodded and nudged down four potatoes of different shape and color from a hanging basket, and started chopping, "oh and make'em hot" tuck added as he stepped back to rejoin Burgundy who was still taking it all in.
"How," Burgundy said, low, because he could not help it. "How do they grow this? we don't have farms anywhere and there's basically no sun half the year. I thought we shipped in all our food."
Tuck grinned.

"So yes, all *YOUR food *is shipped in, the fancy meat and fruits from other planets. But *our *food" he looked and nodded at the women who was scoring the potato and rubbing it with salt and some tan colored powder,  "it grows down here. And you were wrong. We *do *have farms. They're just not above ground.
"They're in the mines?"
"Yeah, I mean not like *in *the mines where they work, tha'd be crazy and messy but yeah like down there." Tuck nodded faintly at the ground, rubbing his hands to warm up.
"But wait, how? How do they get their energy with no sun?"

"I don't know how it works, Ghost, you nerd," Tuck said laughing.  "Somethin' with the trees. The scrub trees up top, the ugly ones? Their roots go down and the mushroom roots down there come up, and they meet in the middle and they trade."
"They trade?"

"Yeah something like that, the mushroom brings something up, the tree gives it something back. My grandpa used to go on about it when he was teaching me to cook back in the day. Said the mushrooms were like cargo ships." He grinned. "Little ships in the rock, running energy down from the sun to make our farms work. He liked that one, and I did too when I was like *six*"
He paused catching back up to Burgundy's question

"But yeah I don't know it works Ghost, you're the one who went to all that school, I just know they're down there. And they're huge. Like rows and rows of green, most of it hanging from the ceiling of rooms in the rock, mostly old spots they'd mine but that ran dry or somethin'. And yeah, now we farm'em. "  He continued  "Peppers, mostly. That's what we grow. There's like, I don't know, nine hundred kinds of peppers? More? Every color you think of, there's a pepper."

Burgundy was making a connection to one of his father's recurring dinner performances which went something like*You know what nobody understands about Dross?*  *They think it's a  wasteland. Frozen, starving planet, nothing here. They're wrong!  The best food in the system. Easily. Abundance like nowhere else. *
Burgundy had thought it was one of his insecure delusions but now he realized his father was absolutely correct.
The woman was done with their, what was it, Hot Umberroots, and handed them to Tuck who placed down two coins just as the man had done. Then he gave the paper wrapped bundle to Burgundy.
Steam was racing off the bundle into the frigid air. The medallions of roots were too hot to eat, their oil still dancing on the skin. Burgundy looked around.

The people here ate well and laughed at each other's sons and smiled and his father knew it, and had built a life on top of it in which none of *this* ever came up his hill except the meat, twice a year, and the boast, at dinner, to strangers.
"Eat one Ghost. Quickly before they gets cold." Tuck said.

Making sure his face was still mostly hidden from view, Burgundy bit into one of the black oblong medallions. He had never tasted anything like it. The outside had gone past crisp to almost burnt, and it shattered, and under it the flesh was soft and sweet. Then the spice arrived a beat behind the sweetness, dark and smoky, and then the heat, blooming up the back of his throat until his eyes ran and he had to breathe through his mouth, and it was wonderful. He dipped the second half into the yogurt sauce and ate it. A bright explosion of creamy herby flavor, and some relief to his burning tongue.
And that's when he sensed a flavor that rung familar,

"That heat you're tasting, that's scarr-pepper. That's famous even on other planets because it only grows here, and that one *does* end up in my kitchen, I mean *your* kitchen–– Ha! You know what I mean." he laughed, but it was forced, followed by an awkward silence,
Burgundy did know what he meant. He had eaten scarr-pepper his whole life, in food made by hands he never saw. Or thought about.
Burgundy looked at Tuck's hand holding the waxed paper of fried roots. A burn scar across two knuckles, old and shining.

Neither of them said anything for a moment. Then Tuck balled up the empty wax paper and tossed it in a fire drum and said, "Come on. Ran's this way, lots more to see" and the moment closed over like it was nothing. Tuck turned and walked back into the sea of people.
They went up through the market slowly, because Burgundy would not go fast. He had never been let alone inside this much real life.
A man sold cups of something they called scald, a hot dark brew thick as broth, ladled from a dented pot half a man's height, into tins you drank and handed back.

A grandmother worked a pot of something red and slow, dropping in the small bold-red potatoes that looked like near perfect spheres, and the smell of it was the spice he had not been able to name from the top of the stair.

Children ran the lanes between the fires with no coats on, screaming after eachother. Nobody stopped them. Everywhere the steam went up and hung and turned to gold in the low light, and everywhere, under the food and the talk, there was something else he noticed only half way through.
It was the machines. They were everywhere, once he saw the first one, and he could not stop seeing them after.

The first one he stopped to stare at was at a stall where a very old man pouring a thin baige batter onto a flat skillet slicked with fat, where it spread and set and blistered, he folded greens and slivered peppers into the fold and pressed it flat with the back of a blade until the edges went crisp, and between orders he cleaned the surface with a ladle of water from a metal jug.
At the foot of his stove, mounted to a metal bar, a fan, taken ouf of an old engine and repurposed here to spin air slowly onto the coals, gently making them glow.

When the man's water ran low he reached back without looking and clicked a small switch, and the fan stopped. Now the motor was turning a small pump mounted to the other side of the same bar, the pump pulling meltwater up a hose into his metal jug. He looked away, bored as he let it fill. Then he clicked the switch back and the pump stopped and the fan started up again, feeding the fire. One motor that did one thing or the other, never both.

"You've got'em on the one motor," Burgundy said. He had not meant to say it out loud. But he did try to adopt the slang. He kept going, "Both of them, off the one. So you can only ever run the one at a time. The fire, or the water."

The old man did not look up from his skillet. He flipped the folded batter, pressed it, let the edge crisp. "Can't blow on a fire with no one to feed." Burgundy wasn't sure what he meant, and he moved on. Luckily Tuck hadn't seen the interaction.

Further on, a mom had run a length of copper gutter down off a warm roof, where the meltwater came steady, and set a wheel under the fall of it. The wheel was an old mine drill rotor with small tin cups riveted around the rim, and the water dropped into the cups and turned it. Fast. And the axle ran back through a train of mismatched gears into a coil of wire wound on a nail-studded spool. A single bulb hung off the end of the whole thing, burning steady over the woman as she fed her newborn off her chest.
"You're doing it again," Tuck said. "That thing with your face, which by the way you need to cover better"
"What thing."
"Like every busted fan and light bulb is a miracle." He steered him on by the sleeve. "It's a fan, Ghost. It blows on a fire. My nan had one. Everyone's nan had one."

But Burgundy could not stop. Up the hill, in the palace, a fan that broke got carried off by a man whose whole job was carrying off broken things, and a new one came from a crate, and no one ever saw where the crate came from or where the broken one went.
Down here nothing went anywhere. It got opened up and stared at and made into the next thing.
"Everyone's nan had one?" Burgundy said. "Nobody in the palace could build anything like this."
"Course they couldn't." Tuck said it like it was obvious, and to him it was. "They don't have to."

They passed a woman feeding peppers into a mill rigged to an old sewing table. She was controlling the grind with a rocking pedle she was pumping with one foot under the table, the drive belt that was patched in two places with wire and so it did not quite run true, and the whole rig ticked once each turn.
She kept the rhythm without looking, both hands feeding dried peppers into the grinder's hopper, red dust coming out the bottom into a metal bucket and wafting into the street.

But the one that held him longest was near the top of the stair, where the stalls began to thin. A boy no older than Burgundy sat framed by a thin doorway, behind a machine no bigger than a loaf of bread on a small wooden table. Beside it sat a basket of copper wire, salvaged, a rat's nest of kinked and tangled wire, the ends gone green. His little contraption was feeding in wire from the tangle on one side and channeling it out the other, winding it tightly around a spool in tight even rows.

The boy was not watching it. He was eating a strip of fried red potato, one-handed, watching the lane, while turning the crank the drove the machine's delicate movement through a series of mismatched gears.
Burgundy had been winding coils by hand in the basement for four months. His were lumpy and uneven, and he wound and unwound and rewound them, and he hated every hour of it.
He stood in front of the boy's machine and did not say anything. His eyes feasted on the build.
"You need something?" the boy said, not friendly, one hand holding a fried root drenched in sauce.
"Relax, Thresher, he's not buying." Tuck was already pulling Burgundy off by the sleeve. "He just likes staring at junk. Don't let it go to your head."
The boy looked at Burgundy a second longer, decided he was harmless, and went back to the lane.
"Ok we're done staring at things" Tuck said, a note of increased vigilance in his voice.
"We gotta get to Ran's and then get back."
They came to the end of the stalls. The market noise fell away behind them and then. A big empty square.
At the head of the square stood a tall ornate building, made of warm stone with a row of tall doors, the Custom House, where the crown ran the operation that weighed and shipped the Ore.

And in the middle, stood a statue three times the height of a man: Burgundy's grandfather, a decade dead, cast in dark metal, one hand out over the empty square, a minecart by his side with markings Burgundy knew was the language of the Ghai

Near the foot of the statue a ring was painted on the stone White once, flaking now, wide as a house. Inside stood two tall grey soldiers, masked helmets, standing still, the only other people in the square.

"Nicholas's men," Tuck said, low, as they walked along the edge of the square. The ease had gone out of his voice. "It's collection day tomorrow. They always send a few of their men here a day early to just, I dunno. Their helmets never come off, they just stand there in their little rings, all night, all day, until the big  ships come to collect–– the stuff."
*The Stuff*. Tuck didn't know the word 'tribute.' nor all it meant.

"And we're not allowed to cross into that circle." He said, "No, no. Bad news if you do. My neighbors uncle went into one once. Drunk, years back, to be funny or somethin'. Put his hand on a soldier and kissed its mask. And it ended poorly for him"

Tuck sped up their walking and his eyes tracked the soldiers. "His whole family had their stipend cut for 20 days, and the guy–– the uncle, was gone by morning. Not killed that anyone saw. Just, gone."

He shrugged,  "My mom says Nicholas is the reason no one invades Dross and to just be grateful and not mess with them. But if I ever meet the guy I'm gunna tell him to chill out with these soldiers. They're not just here, there's a bunch all over the city."."
They left the square, and after two more turns they were standing in front of a house made of scrap. Walls made of tin sheets and old doors and a section of ship's hull, all lapped over each other.

A yard opened off the side of it behind a fence of stacked drums, and the yard was full. Heaped really.  Seemingly sorted, but into hills: a hill of motors, a hill of rats nest wire, a hill of pipe furred white with frost.
Smoke came up thin from a pipe in the roof. And someone moved inside.
"Ran's!" Tuck said.

chapters.title: Ran's
paragraphs: "Tuckey my guy!" Ran belted when he opened the door to them. "How you doing partner? Your mom send you with anything special for me?" Ran asked.

Tuck pulled from his bag a purple fruit like the ones Burgundy would occasionally see sliced at breakfast, and passed it to Ran. "Nice!" He eyed it, "Another one of these fancy fruits you all eat up there. Beautiful. Oh come in." and then he took a bite and turned "And who's this?" he said through a mouthful of the purple fruit.
