paragraphs: At breakfast the next morning he found his mother at the small table by the east window, tea and a book, the way she sat before the palace woke. The morning was crisp and she was looking at the rising sun, one of the last before the Freeze would come and keep the sun glued to the horizon all day.
"I want to come on the next shipment," he said.
She closed her book and looked at him. "Why?"
"I've been taking from your family's shipments for two years and I've never once seen it. I want to know how it works." He sat down across from her. "And I want to meet your cousin."
She looked at him over the cup for a moment, reading him.

"Understanding the family trade is technically part of your princely duties," she said. "Your father would approve of the interest, if you asked him, which you won't need to." She went back to the book. "The next one is in three days. And Ressa may or may not be there."
"It will be a leaner year after this one," she said. "A Vicentennial year. Everything gets looked at harder, even ours. If there is something you are going to need, think of it now."

Burgundy spent the next three days welding three cube chambers to his DREKKOs, preparing to house a sphere of osmarine. On the third night his mother came by his chamber doors at dark and told him to follow.

Burgundy spent the next three days welding three cube chambers to his DREKKOS, preparing to house a sphere of Osmarine. On the third night his mother came by his chamber doors at dark and told him to follow.

They walked through the quiet palace lit by lanterns and toward the north gate, where a guard opened it without looking at either of them, then along a path running east, toward the low ground beyond the cargo field where the tribute loaded. Burgundy had assumed ships came down on Dross in exactly one place. But he had been wrong.

There was a second cargo field. Smaller. Lit only by amber lanterns set low along its edges. A freight ship sat on the landing pad, dark except for a few small utility lights no bigger than lamp-wicks.
This was not one of Nicholas's grey giants, which never landed at all. This was much smaller, maybe ten percent the size. It was scuffed, patched, resting on wheels. Its cargo ramp was down.
People dressed in dark clothing rolled crates up the ramp on dollies..
Burgundy and Mira approached the ramp just as a woman was walking down it out of the ship to meet them. She was carrying a clipboard under her  arm.  Was this Ressa, his mother's cousin?

She held the clipboard out to Mira. "Manifest's ready. Ressa signed the outbound this afternoon.  The medicine order is short two pallets. The vendor's problem, not ours." So this wasn't Ressa, but rather one of her people.  His mother's cousin ran the trade without attending it. Then, with a glance at Burgundy that lasted no more than a half a second the woman said, "Is this—"
"Yes," Mira said.
The woman snuck one more glance at Burgundy then turned back up the ramp signaling to the loaders to proceed.
Mira began focusing on the papers on the clipboard, scanning each line and occasionally signing her name.
Burgundy watched the ship.

Up the ramp went the crates of ore. He knew it by the markings now: density codes, grade markings, black corvite in sealed bundles. And beside the ore, in a separate stack the crews handled differently, more slowly, in padded cradles: casks. Small. Banded with metal. When a loader tilted one to seat it on the sled, the seam of the lid showed a faint glow, cold and steady.

He knew what it was. He had heard the word over the years. Mostly in a whisper: Cinder. A mind altering drug. The substance that fueled the spiritual dimension of the Midsteam Descent. Refined from a rare deep seam mineral called Cindrite in a method the Ghai discovered. Flecks of the purified metal were ground with the tunnel mushroom and then consumed as a tea that glowed pale blue. Cinder was sacred in the old rituals but illegal in every system. And yet there was a black market for it throughout the whole galaxy. It was a stimulant that ran a man for two days and gave him blissful visions. This was Dross's second harvest, their metal cash crop that funded the King's vanity projects.
The casks went up, and the ore behind them, and Burgundy watched it climb the ramp, and the question came out of him before he had decided to ask it.
"Do you trade osmarine?" he said to the woman

Mira looked up from her clipboard at Burgundy and then to the woman, who laughed, once, before she remembered who she was laughing at. "Do we trade osmarine?" She shook her head. "Nobody 'trades' osmarine. The Alliance and Nicholas hold every gram between here and the core. There is not a fleck of it loose anywhere, and anyone who tells you different is a conman."
His mother was listening, not looking up from the clipboard.

"Nicholas has soldiers in the four mines that harvest it on Dross," Mira said, "His own men, permanently, on our ground. They watch the miners, day and night, and at the ramp they weigh it to the gram, and it leaves on his ship and no others." She initialed a line. "So, no. We do not have access to osmarine."
Burgundy nodded, and looked back at the ship.
"What do you need osmarine for?" the woman on the ramp said.
"Oh nothing, just curious how it works," Burgundy said, and then stayed quiet as the shipment went on.

Down the ramp came the arriving cargo. Burgundy had expected the incoming cargo to be illicit items like drugs or weapons. But instead he saw seed stock in heavy sacks. Casks of cooking oil, sacks of grain marked in a language he couldn't read. But also luxury items for the palace. Cooler crates likely full of special meats from other worlds. This stuff would end up on his plate at dinner. He had never wondered its origins.

After an hour of loaders going back and forth he saw a familiar stack of boxes of all sizes: Coils of special wire, drill heads wrapped in oiled paper, motors the size of fists nested in foam and what he craved most: the small wooden boxes he knew contained crystal discs from the Core world, packed tightly between wool and sawdust.

It was worrisome to have it all out in the open like this. The crew carrying his secret down the ramp on dollys like any other shipment. But when he really thought about it, he realized that to them this was just another crate. It may look suspicious to his father, but his father didn't ever come to these shipments. According to Mira, he hadn't for years. He preferred Mira to be the interface.
Mira looked at one of the crew and said "Lew." and nodded her head at the bundle of Burgundy's items.
Lew must have been the insider that Mira paid to get all this from the cargo field to the white room behind the bookshelf. He had no idea what kind of arrangement they had but he trusted it was safe.
Lew gave almost no acknowledgment that he had heard but went straight to gather the boxes and crates onto a motorized loader, and off he went into the dark.

Mira was finishing on the clipboard now. She initialed a line. She stopped at another. "This count is wrong. There were only seventeen casks." The woman on the ramp checked; agreed. Mira corrected it herself, small precise figures, the same hand that labeled the toolbox drawers in the white room.

While she worked down the last pages he drifted to the rope line at the field's edge and looked out. The low city lay below in its scattered lights, small and warm against the dark, and at the very bottom of the slope, where everything else went black, one thin strip burned brighter than the rest.
The night market at the bottom of the city.

He could almost smell it from here, four years gone. The frying roots, the red spice. Tuck ahead of him in the crowd with his hands in his pockets. The singing cook, the heat of the fires and steam, the whole loud warm world of it going on down there right now without him.
*You're underselling it,* he had said, fifteen years old, forgetting his accent. *It's worth ten times that. There's osmarine sealed in the core.*
*You're underselling it,* he had said, fifteen years old, forgetting his accent. *It's worth ten times that. There's osmarine sealed in the core.*
*There's osmarine sealed in the core.*
He stood very still at the rope line.

The cage-lifts. No motor on Dross could haul tons of ore a kilometer straight up, so every cage carried a governor core bolted under its floor, a sealed housing with a little low-grade osmarine inside, canceling most of the load's weight so the winch lifted only the difference. He had known that since he was a boy. He had never once thought about what it meant.

Cores got knocked loose. And because they half-float, they would fall wrong, drifting sideways into old unused shafts. Gone forever, that is until miners would inevitably stumble upon them, and sell them to the local scrap yard. Ran.  Who stacked cores, thick with green patina, on a high shelf not knowing exactly what he had.
The most controlled substance in the galaxy was sitting in a junk man's house, priced as tin.
His mother closed the clipboard. The loaders were dragging the ramp chains loose.
Burgundy's gaze was fixed on the city below.
He was going to need to see Ran.

chapters.title: Tuck
paragraphs: During the Freeze, the palace turned back into a beacon of heat: every window lit, the boilers running day and night, and around its foundations a ring of bare wet stone where the snow could not lie. The only melted thing in sight.

The cold storage was the only cold room in the palace. Down in the wood-paneled room the size of a full bedroom, the walls wept frost and your breath stood in the air in front of you, the same as it did outside.

Racks ran floor to ceiling on three walls. Sacks of tubers, wheels of hard cheese, stout crocks of butter stacked like masonry. A whole shelf of desserts waiting on their plates, custards and dark tortes glazed to a shine. And along the back wall, on iron hooks, the fen-buck from the preserve, skinned and split and hanging in their parts, shoulder and haunch and saddle, each piece still keeping the shape of the animal it had been.
Burgundy waited at the back racks, behind wheels of cheese.
He only waited ten minutes before Tuck entered and went to fill a sack with tubers.
"Hey, Tuck," Burgundy said, stepping out from behind the rack.
"What the—" he squinted into the dark "Ghost? Is that you? What in the—"
"I need your help Tuck."
Tuck's face softened to something familiar to Burgundy. And he smiled..
"Oh man, Ghost, you're up to something *again?"*
"Yes"

"What? more robots? Still?" He laughed a big laugh and Burgundy smiled. "You're still doin' that even though you've become all princely now? Man I thought you were done. That you were done forever. I see you going to the big meeting every morning. Hunting with the men? Even the kitchen heard that you missed the buck twice. I figured you just didn't wanna shoot one."
"Tuck," Burgundy said. "I need to visit Ran."

Tuck let out a breath that hung white between them. Then he laughed again. "Man sorry, Ghost, I just can't believe it. Can't believe you're here. Not gunna lie, I grieved you man. Thought you had changed forever and turned into one of them." Tuck had never called Burgundy's family one of them before. Burgundy understood why he would now.
Tuck set down the sack of tubers he was carrying and said "yeah course I'll take you to Ran's. Securities a bit trickier than when we used to sneak about. But I have a way"
"Thanks Tuck. I really appreciate it"
"Course, let's meet in the old wine cellar when the moons are full, five days from now. The guards always get drunk under full moons. I'll make sure they get the strong stuff this week"

Then Tuck dug two fingers into his apron pocket and came out with a small folded square of cloth, brown cotton gone soft with washing. "Here. From our birthdays." He put it in Burgundy's hand. "Cut it back in the Steam. Been carrying it since." He shrugged, and re-shouldered his sack.
Burgundy nodded and Tuck started back up the stairs toward the warmth. "And Ghost," he said on his way up "really good to see you again."
"You too Tuck.
"You too Tuck.""
Five nights later Tuck and Burgundy met in the old wine cellar.

Burgundy handed over his own square before either of them said anything else: heavy wool, clan red, cut that afternoon from the inside hem of his council coat. Tuck turned it over once, and looked at it a second longer than he needed to, and put it away in his coat.
"Ok we're going out the service entrance, where we get our food shipments. I'm gunna put you in one of the big long wooden crates the cheese wheels come in, and dolly you out of the gate"
"And the guards?"
"Remember, they're drinking tonight, I personally delivered some barley liquor that will have them laughing at the moons when we pass. They won't ask to check anything"
Tuck's plan worked exactly as he envisioned. Soon Burgundy was climbing out of the wooden crate on the side of the path that led from the palace to the town.

The path lay in the long dusk of the Freeze, the sun somewhere behind the hills where it would stay for months, the snow holding the last of the light. The moons did the sun's work, and every man on the path threw two shadows, blue across the drifts. They walked quickly, collars up, boots squeaking on the pack.
"So what's all this prince business, then," Tuck said. "Meetings every morning. Hunts. The coat."
"It's an act."
"An act."

"It keeps my father not asking questions. Or ever knowing what I'm actually doing" He watched his breath go up. "Which I'm not going to tell you about. The less you know, the less danger you're in. You're in enough just walking me down this hill."
Tuck stopped walking for a second. "Danger?" He caught back up. "What are you doing, Ghost? How serious is this thing?"
Burgundy said nothing.

They came into the low city through the night market. Burgundy wore the same laborer's coat, a scarf up over his face, and through the wool the smells came anyway, the frying roots, the red spices, the smoke off the stone ovens, and for a few steps he was fifteen again and the whole warm loud world was his to walk through.
Nobody looked at them. The Freeze kept every head down and every scarf up. Being nobody was easy in the cold.

Ran's yard sat where it had always sat, the heaps taller under the snow, the paths between them beaten to ice. Tuck knocked, and pushed the door open on the same stove-warmth, the same pepper pot, the same walls of jars.
"Uncle. Brought a customer."
Ran came out from the back room wiping his hands on a rag. He saw Tuck and started to smile. Then Burgundy pulled the scarf down.
Ran went still. The rag stopped moving in his hands. His eyes locked on Burgundy's face.
"Tuck." His voice was careful. "What is this."
"Uncle, it's fine, it's—Ghost you weren't supposed to—"
"I'm here to buy," Burgundy said. "That's all." He nodded at the high shelf, at the basket sitting where a basket had sat for four years. "The governor cores. All of them."
Ran looked at him a long moment. Then he barked, once, half a laugh and half something else, and dug two fingers into his vest pocket, and came out with a coin, and slammed it flat on the counter.

"I knew it." He left his finger on the coin. It was old and rubbed and it had the King's face on it, stamped young. "You paid me with a coin just like this, four years back. And after you walked out of here talkin' like a book with your fancy accent, I sat with it under the lamp, and I looked at the face on the coin, and thought I was mad." He took his finger off it, his face locked in a furrowed brow.

He got the stool and lifted the basket down, one-handed, far too easily, the way no basket of metal should come down, and set it on the counter where it sat a little too lightly. Twelve spheres, each the size of a big man's fist, crusted green with age, and where the crust had flaked away, thin veins of some translucent metal ran through the shells, catching the lamplight like frozen water.

"Twelve now," Ran said. "After what you said that day, I put word down the shafts. Any man finds one of the floaters in the old workings, drifted off into some shaft where it's got no business, bring it to Ran, Ran pays fair."

He turned one under the lamp, not quite letting it go. "Never cracked one. Don't really know what I'd do with low grade osmarine.  But I collected 'em, on the word of a boy I met once." He set it back and looked up, and the wariness came back into his face. "And now the boy's back. And I gotta say I'm not feelin' too great about selling you a prohibited substance at the moment"
"Uncle," Tuck said. "Come on. He's not going to do anything bad with them."
"You told me yourself he'd gone all royal. Sittin' the meetings. Doin' the hunts n' all. Your words, Tuck, not mine."
"Yeah, I thought that. It's not real. It's a show he's putting on."
"And how would you be sure of that."
"Because" Tuck paused "I know him," he said, looking at Burgundy.

Ran looked at his nephew a moment. Then Burgundy took the sack from inside his coat and set it on the counter and opened the neck of it. Gold, his father's face over and over in the lamplight. A pile of coins, surely more than the yard turned in a season.
Ran looked at the money and did not touch it.

"I'll ask you one thing straight," he said, " What are you buildin'. Because if it's some new way to hold this city down, we're full up. You understand me? It can't be held any harder than it's held. They took Nate two days back. My friend thirty years. Down the hole. For months probably."

"And you know what for? Talkin'. On shift, to his own crew, about the state of the lower shafts, dismal working conditions. And someone on that crew rats him out, and just like that he was thrown into the hole." He wiped his hands on the rag again "That's what it is here now. Every man watchin' his own mouth. So you tell me what you're buildin', or the basket goes back on the shelf, gold or no gold."
"It's not for control," Burgundy said.
"So says the crown prince in my shop."
"My father doesn't know I'm here." Burgundy said it flat.  "And I'll tell you what else he doesn't know, because he's never once asked. He doesn't know TKTKTK

I've sat there for more than two years listening to the men who run this planet talk about you and your neighbors like a herd of animals that needs to be fenced. And I've sat there and said nothing, because saying something up there actually fixes nothing down here." He looked at the basket, and then back at Ran. "Everyone in that palace spends their cleverness keeping this city exactly where it is. I'm spending mine another way. That's as much as I'll tell you. Now are you selling these cores or not?"

The stove ticked. Tuck had gone quiet. Ran looked at Burgundy for a long time, the way he had once looked at a boy pricing scrap, and whatever he was searching for, he must have found some of it, because he pulled the sack of gold toward him without counting it, and tipped the twelve cores one by one into a grain sack, rags folded between them so they would not knock.  He pushed it across the counter.
"Make something worth what it cost," he said.

chapters.title: Digging
paragraphs: He had the cores for a week before he found the nerve to crack one.

They sat in the grain sack Tuck had dollied through the gate, twelve of them. And every time he passed the bench he picked one up and set it down again. Fist-sized, crusted green, lighter in the hand than a thing that size had any right to be. He knew what the lightness was now. He had read the passage off the disc until the dense core-world words came apart in his mouth: *a refined antibarytic element, resistance at the tool face returned as forward impulse, no platform mass required, the effect amplified when the element was held spinning. *Ran had called it *the stuff that floats*.
So he sawed one open, cutting through the tin until the two curved halves fell open. And inside it, an ivort white sphere, mounted into a cradle with a spinning mechanism.

There was already a small perfect hole drilled through the center of the sphere. Where the spinners could grip it. He mounted the sphere into the cage he had welded, onto the back of the DREKKOs, the cage now clad with magnets, He flipped one switched inside the cage and the sphere started to spin inside the mount.   The report had called this moment *magnetically suspended rotation.*
He walked wheeled this first DREKKO over to the corvite face that had thrown it a week ago, the same seam, the same chisel point set true along it. Current on.
He gave the drive command.

The treads stood still on the stone as the machine started pushing forward into the rock. The reaction that used to push the machine backward, now went up the arm and into the spinning sphere of osmarine and back down into the bit, and the chisel walked into the rock instead. A wafer of corvite the size of his thumb split off along the seam, dropped, and rang once against the floor of the robot's empty bucket.
He sat down on the cold floor where he had watched it lose so many times, and listened to the drill go on into the rock, and for one long breath it was the finest thing he had ever made.

He spent the next week rigging all three of his DREKKOs with osmarine spheres in the cage he wleded inside their chest. He rigged two per robot and calculated that this increased each DREKKO's mass by seven thousand percent.
As he put the robots to work on the wall, he started to notice what would become his final challenge: The robots got stuck.
As he put the robots to work on the wall, he started to notice what would become his final challenge. The robots got stuck.

He saw it first on a single machine, on a night he was too tired to intervene. It had found a seam, set the chisel  along it, and begun to work, but the seam was not giving. A harder machine had never existed on this planet. It drove the point in with the force of something fifty times its size, and the corvite held anyway, the way corvite sometimes did, and the machine's answer was to do it again. Same point, same angle..

He sat against the wall and watched it strike that dead seam forty times, patient as a clock, and understood that it would strike it four hundred times, four thousand, all night and into the morning, because nothing in it could conclude the one thing a twelve-year-old shaft boy would have concluded in a minute: this seam is done, move on.
And once he had seen it in one, he saw it in all of them.
They could sense everything. The two eyes read the face and picked the tool and set the angle, and the code he was proudest of scored every action as it happened.
But the data wasn't coming back to improve the code. They could grade their own work and could not learn from the grade, could not do more than the few blunt adjustments he had written in by hand.
And so each machine climbed for a week or two and then settled onto a competence that never became mastery.

Every real improvement still ran through him, his read of the log, his rewrite, his upload, one tired hand feeding data and feedback to three tireless bodies. All the force the osmarine gave them, and they spent it doing the same wrong thing harder.

He knew, from the discs, that he was not the only one stuck here. Three labs in the core worlds had been circling this exact problem for years. How to build a machine that did not just sense and score but *learned*, folded every action back into itself, so that each swing taught the next swing and the improving itself improved.

The papers agreed it was coming. The papers had been agreeing for a decade, from inside clean labs, on simple rigs, in air scrubbed of dust and heat. Nobody had cracked it there. He certainly had not cracked it here.
He shut the machines down one at a time, and the cell went quiet, and the seam the first one had been worrying all night stood in the lamplight, barely scarred.
The strongest digging machines ever built on Dross. And worth nothing, none of it, until they could teach themselves to get better.

chapters.title: The Lounge
paragraphs: His father had never once asked him into the lounge.
It sat off the private wing, a long room Burgundy had walked past a thousand times and entered never, until tonight.

The first thing he noticed was the light. Most of it came from lanterns with amber shades set low along the walls, so the whole room stood in a honey-colored glow that rounded the edges of everything and made the leather chairs shine like chestnuts. Between the lanterns, on low tables and in wall brackets, hung globes of corvite ground thin enough to pass light, each a different shade, one the blue-black of a deep bruise, one nearly violet, one the green of pond ice, glowing cold and small against all that warm.

The carpet took his boots to the ankle. The cushions heaped in the chairs were velvet, deep red, stitched in a fine close hand he knew, though it took him a moment to place it, and when he placed it he wished he had not. Essa's hand. The old woman had sewn for this palace until the Freeze took her, and here was her work, propping up the men who ruled the planet.

His father sat in the largest chair with a glass at his elbow, and Oz sat across from him, and each of them held a cigar of a leaf Burgundy had never seen, rolled thick as a thumb, the wrapper a dark green gone orange at the edges with a thread of gold running its length.
The smoke came off it heavier than woodsmoke and sweeter, and hung in the amber light in slow blue sheets.

"These come from a jungle world in a different system", his father said proudly about his cigar "A place that grows a hundred leaves and every does something different you." He laughed and looked at Oz who chuckled along.  He waved at a box of them on the table. Burgundy did not take one.
"Sit," his father said, pleased. "You're old enough now to join us from here for out little...chats." He smiled at Oz.

The King had invited Burgundy tonight promising that this was the *real council,* where the real decisions about security were made. And then he gave a speech about *developing discernment over where formality and process actually hinder progress. *
So he came, and sat and he listened.
Oz talked the way he moved, without hurry. But his voice picked up urgency when he gave the king the update on the security situation.
"More groups tonight," Oz said. "The south this time. Bolder than I'd like."
"Bolder how," the King said.
"There's talk of a stop-work. Three of the deeper levels." Oz said.  "Messages passed at shift change, world of mouth. Nothing written. "
The word sat over the table. Nobody at council had said *strike* in Burgundy's lifetime, and Oz did not say it now.
"We have a minder down there. He reported it right away and we took care of it. We took two or three of the offenders.

"It's always a few," his father said, comfortable, turning the cigar in his fingers. "A few who would rather pull the whole roof down than carry their share of it. The rest are good. They want to feed their families and be left alone. Our work is to see that the few never teach the many to be so full of hate and resentment." He said it kindly, and Burgundy sat on Essa's cushions in the honey light and felt a new feeling that was becoming familiar to him, the one from the preserve, from the grain scattered in the clearing.
Then, gathering his papers, as an afterthought: "Oh, and we took one more tonight. A scrap dealer, up in Kettletown. He was hoarding osmarine."
The King's head came up. "What.?"
"Osmarine, sire. Low grade, but real."
"How does a Kettletown junk man come by osmarine."

"Governor cores." Oz squared the pages against the table. "The lift cores. The ones under the cage floors, that carry the harvest up the shafts. He'd been collecting them whole. Paying good coin for every one that came through his door."
"And how are lift cores ending up in a scrap yard."

"They get knocked loose, from time to time. A cage slams, a coupling goes, and the core drops off and drifts away into the dead shafts. It's not new. What's new is that this man had put a call out saying he'd pay a good price for any found floaters."
"Floaters. And who was he selling the stuff to?"

"The cores weren't in his shop. Sold on, we judge. Who to, we haven't found." Oz laid a folded paper on the table. "But he'd done well for a junk man. There was a strongbox under his floor. Fresh-minted gold."

His father picked up the paper, read it, set it down. The good humor had gone flat out of his voice. "Someone is buying loose osmarine off a Kettletown scrap man," he said. "I don't know who, and I don't know what for, and I dislike both of those. Find me the buyer."
There was a silence while the men puffed their cigars.
Burgundy sat very still in the honey light. hit heart was going so hard he was sure the thud of it was visible through his shirt.

They had Ran. Ran was in a hole somewhere in the dark right now. And they were looking for the buyer and the buyer was him.  Would ran tell his interrogators that the prince showed up with freshly minted gold and bought twelve governor cores?
He needed to move. He needed to get up from this chair without running.

He made himself count ten. Then he set his hands on the arms of the chair and said he was tired, that council came early. His father waved the cigar in a small arc that was half blessing and half dismissal.
"Go to bed. You did well today.  You listened, that is most of ruling." He was already turning back to Oz.
Burgundy walked out of the lounge at the pace of a tired prince, down the corridor and around the corner, and then he was running.

He went down the back stairs two at a time and through the cold rooms and came into the kitchens still in his good coat, and a dozen faces lifted from their work and went still. It was late. A few of them were left, scrubbing the long tables. They looked at the prince standing in their doorway breathing hard with something wrong in his face, and none of them said anything.
He looked around for Tuck who was at the sink, just looking over his should.
paced across the kitchen and Burgundy and pulled Tuck by the sleeve and pulled him out into the passage, where the stone was cold and the light was thin.
"They took Ran," he said.
"I know," Tuck said.
It stopped him. "You know?"
"Word came up an hour ago. His neighbor's boy runs the milk to the east gate." Tuck's face was concerned and scared.

"It's because of me." The words were out before he could weigh them. "He collected the cores because of me. I told him what they were worth, four years ago, and he believed me and put the word out and gathered them, and I went back and bought every one, and tonight they came for him." The corridor held still around the two of them.
Tuck did not tell him it was not his fault. That was the thing Burgundy would remember, later, in the dark. Tuck had never been in the business of comfortable lies, and he did not start now.
"Is there anything you can do to get him out?" Tuck said. Burgundy knew there wasn't.
"I...I don't know Tuck" he said shaking his head.
They looked at each other in silence a long moment.
Burgundy went back up through the palace to his own wing, past the guard who did not look at him, and shut the door of his chamber, and lay down on the bed in his clothes.
He had thought of it as his. His secret, his risk, his machines, a thing that touched no one but himself. But it wasn't just him anymore.

The weight of what he had done came down on him in the dark, and for the first time since the yellow book swung open on the white room he did not think about the machines at all. He turned his face into the pillow and cried, quietly, so the guard outside the door would not hear.

chapters.title: Closed Loop Embodiment
paragraphs: He did not sleep. He lay in his clothes on the bed where he had cried himself empty.
Then he went over the problem again. Every version ended the same way.

He could not go to his father. If he asked the King to release Ran, his father would ask why the prince cared about a scrap dealer in Kettletown. The answer would lead to the hidden bookcase, the white room, and the two years Burgundy had spent buying parts in secret.
When Burgundy could not solve a problem, he worked.

So before the clock struck midnight he spring out of his bed and rushed through the dark palace toward his dungeon-turned-lab where he had been circling the same problem for weeks.  Robots that would not teach themselves to improve.

A new batch of discs painted a picture of Core-world teams in top labs, three of them, working the same problem from different directions. How they had begun successfully testing robotics whose own sensors fed the machine's own learning.

Every strain gauge and thermal reading and torque curve pouring data into the code's scoring functions in real time, the way a hot lantern teaches a child's hand: touch it once, and the brain rewrites itself so you never touch it again.

The papers called it *closed-loop embodiment*. He had read the twelve of them until he saw the code in his sleep. And somewhere in the reading he had understood something: These researchers had proved all this only in clean labs, on simple rigs, in air scrubbed of the dust and heat and the physics that made his machines choke.

None of them had ever spent a night on their back under a machine with sealant on their hands. They were brilliant but they were blind to what they called in the papers: *Real-world industrial application scenarios.*
All he had to do was implement their theories into reality and he would be ahead of them.
He could feel he was arriving at a final frontier. And he could feel that whatever this meant, it would result in some way to free Ran. Or at least ensure his safety until they could let him out.
So he worked the problem.
The sensor buses that fed data from the machine's arms to its brain had been built, by him, in a different life, to report their readings on a fixed cycle to a fixed log.

Now the new learning loop program needed them raw and constant, like a firehose instead of a faucet, a waterfall of real-time data, as constant as human senses flowing into a brain. So with a few lines of code and some rewiring, he opened them up.

But every time he opened the data channels all the way, the processors drowned. The scoring functions fell behind the sensations they were meant to score. The machines got clumsy, worse than before, drunk on their own feeling, and twice that night a drill arm slammed a cutting head into the corvite at an angle that sent shatter pinging off the gallery walls like shrapnel.
He replaced an arm, twice that night. He had done it twenty times by now.

He throttled the flow and it went dull. He batched it and it went blind. He let the machine choose its own sampling rate, which the second paper had hinted at and the third had warned against, and the third paper was right, in a way that cost him a hydraulic line and an hour on his back under the second prototype with sealant drying to a crust on his hands.
Somewhere past the fourth hour he stopped being careful, and he knew he had stopped, and he let it go.
There was a mode he went to when it got late, that he did not trust and could not do without, where the experiments stopped being designed and started being thrown.

He recoded the buses on all three machines in configurations he would not have tried rested, and wrote scoring variants faster than he could test them, and queued them to run in rotation, each machine scoring itself and passing what it learned sideways to the other two.
Then he did the thing he had promised himself he would never do.

He took the micro-charges down off the back shelf. He had built them months ago, a magazine of little explosives the size of beads. Each one meant to be set into a drilled hole and fired to pre-fracture the rock.

These had been too dangerous to him previously but tonight the thing that balked was gone. He fed the dispensers like a cartridge into a slot in the arm and programed their use. He set bounds on the frequency of the charges, and checked the bounds twice, because he was not interested in blowing up the foundations of the palace.

The slit window had gone warm and sharp. Dawn. Council in two hours, and he had not slept. He looked at the three machines idling against the black seam, their green panels pulsing, the queue loaded and waiting on his word, everything he knew and half of what he only guessed set loose at once with no hand on it.
"Go," he said to himself, and pressed the key, and left them working.
He did not look back at the wall. If he had, there would have been nothing to see. Three patient machines, a barely wounded vein.

Council was a blur he moved through with his body while his mind stayed forty feet down, in two places at once, the ran's cell and the seam hi Robots were working on armed with a hundred new experiments.

He got through the grain reports. He got through a dispute between two southern governors. Twice his head dipped, as we nodded off, chin to chest, and the second time he surfaced to a silent room and his father looking at him down the length of the table.
"Am I boring you."
"No, sir. I apologize. I was reading late."
"Reading?"
"The northern field reports." The lie arrived without being sent for. Two years of practice.
His father studied him a moment, then let it go, and Burgundy breathed out slowly, the way you bleed pressure off a line, and under the table his hands would not stay still
"Read earlier" the king said.

It was tribute day. The ships came down at midday. He stood on the platform at his father's right hand and watched Nicholas's ships arrive out of the white sky, three of them, each the length of the palace and its grounds laid end to end. The stopped to hang in the air hundred meters up without wings, without any visible propulsion. Just a deep low pressure that Bunrgundy could feel in his molars.

White arms unfolded from the ships' bellies, joint after joint after joint, and began lifting the thirty-tonne crates in gentle clusters, a month of the planet's blood rising into holds that never showed their insides.

He was so tired the membrane between his two lives had gone to nothing. The day-prince stood in his coat and the night-builder counted joints and thought, helplessly, that if those arms had a feedback loop they would teach themselves to nest the clusters tighter and shave a second off every lift and then a second off the shaving. And behind that thought, the whole time, sat the three machines against the seam and the small sick hope that the explosives had not brought the foundation down, and behind that, Ran.
His head dipped.
He caught it, half a second, and came back to the pressure-hum and the white sky and found his father looking at him. Not with anger. That was the strange thing.
"You're tired," the King said, quietly, under the hum.
"Yes, sir."
His father turned back to the field, and was silent a while, and then, still watching the ships:

"You've become a great prince. I want you to know I see it. You'll be king someday, sooner than either of us would like, how fast years are going. And for the first time I believe you're ready for it. More than ready." He paused. The arms folded themselves away, joint after joint, into the bellies of the ships. "I'm glad you gave up those childish things. The tools and the wires. I know it wasn't easy, but look at you." He nodded at the field, at the order of it, the minerals rising into the sky on schedule. "This suits you. This is right for you. This is what you are."
The ships went up the way the sun crosses a sky, without seeming to move, and were gone. The pressure lifted out of his molars. The cargo field was empty.
"Thank you, Father," he said.
It was, he thought, walking off the platform at his father's side, the kindest thing his father had ever said to him.
He was released an hour before dusk, and by the last of his three routes through the old corridors he was running, coat over his arm, taking the worn stairs down by memory.
He smelled it before he saw it.

Rock dust. In the hallway. Thick, a mineral fog hanging in the light of his lamp, and under it a smell he knew from exactly one place in his life, the rim of a working shaft. Blasting residue. Deep rock, opened.
He came around the last turn into the cell-turned-lab and stopped.
The wall was gone.

chapters.title: Tunnels
paragraphs: Not damaged. Not advanced upon. *Gone*.

Where the seam had been, where months of patient, insufficient chewing had left a shallow scarred tunnel there was now a hole. A real tunnel. Round-shouldered, clean-walled, taller than he was, driven straight into the rock, and so deep that his lantern simply failed inside it, the light falling into the dark the way a stone falls into a well.
The three prototypes were nowhere to be found.

Burgundy stood at the mouth of the tunnel for a long moment, listening to his own pulse beating in his neck, and then he did the thing that years of discipline had built into him: he went to the terminal.
The logs were still streaming across all three screens.

He read standing up, then sitting, then leaning into the screen with both hands on the desk, scrolling, not breathing right. The queue of reckless experiments had run in rotation, as designed, for the first two hours after he had left, variant after variant failing in the old familiar ways, drowned processors, drunk actuators, one logged shatter-event that had cost the second prototype a cutting edge. And then, in the third hour, one configuration on the third machine, one of the ones he had wired past midnight and could barely remember, had *caught*.
Caught was the only word for it. He watched it in the logs the way you watch a spark take to dry grass.

The data firehose and the scoring loop had synchronized. Not throttled, not batched, but brought into rhythm, the machine sampling its own body in rhythm with its own actions, feeling each cut as it made that cut. And the performance line, the line he had been tracking for years, had bent upward.

Then the third machine had passed the configuration sideways to the other two, as designed, and all three lines had bent, and then the loop had begun doing the thing the papers promised could happen but never achieved outside a lab, and Burgundy had never once seen with his own eyes:
It improved the improving.

Every second, the logs said, each machine was taking in its thousands of tiny sensations, torque flutter, thermal bloom, the acoustic signature of rock about to shatter versus rock about to yield, and converting them into micro-adjustments: a cutting angle shaved by a tenth of a degree, a charge from the micro-dispensers placed not where the rock was weakest but where the *next three cuts* would want it weakened, the blast so small and so exact that it did the work of an hour's grinding in a sound no louder than a knuckle crack. And each adjustment fed the next. And the rate of adjustment was itself adjusting. The performance curve in the logs was no longer a line bending. It was a line skyrocketing.
He looked at the numbers at the bottom of the stream, tonnage, waste ratio, energy per kilogram, and he did not believe them.
Then he took his lantern and raced into the tunnel.
The tunnel was beautiful. That was the thing he had not expected. The walls were not rough-bored but *finished*, cut in long smooth strokes that overlapped like the grain of planed wood.

And at intervals along the floor, in neat staged rows, sat the ore. Processed. The machines had not just cut the corvite free; they had pulverized the waste rock and packed it into the walls, leaving a smooth finish. And the corvite itself they had crushed, graded, and pressed into dense dark bundles the size of bread loaves, wrapped in sheeting from their own supply spools and stacked with a regularity that no human crew on Dross had ever achieved or attempted.

He picked one up. It was heavier than it looked. It was worth, at the prices he now knew by heart, more than a southern miner earned in half a year, and there were dozens of them, staged at intervals.

He walked on. The tunnel dipped, and turned, following the vein. He could see where the machines had made choices, where the seam had forked and the cutting pattern showed a moment of exploratory nibbling before committing,  and he had gone perhaps three hundred meters, far beyond any map of the palace foundations, when the character of the walls changed, and he stopped.
The machine-cut smoothness ended at an edge as clean as a doorway.  Beyond it, the tunnel was still a tunnel, but an old one.
Old was not the word. The walls beyond the breach were hand-cut, pick-scarred, the scars softened by centuries of seeping water until they looked less carved than grown.
Water dripped somewhere ahead, a slow mineral music, and the air that moved out of the dark against his face was cave air, wet and unbreathed.
His lantern found the ceiling: soot stains, ancient ones, the ghosts of torch brackets. And on the wall beside the breach, at shoulder height, where a man resting his hand would find it:
Engravings.
He brought the lamp close. Rows of figures, cut shallow and sure: miners with picks, rendered in the blunt confident strokes of people carving their own lives.

And above the figures, repeated, a mark he knew. He had seen it in exactly one place before, in the oldest of the palace's history books, in the chapter every tutor hurried through: a circle within a circle, the inner one filled dark.
The mark of the Ghai.
He stood in the dripping dark with his lamp on the old stone and his education came back to him in pieces.

Before the current line, before his father's family, before the tribute, before Nicholas, there had been a kingdom on Dross, and it had lived *under* the planet rather than on it. The Ghai. A mining people whose answer to a lawless sky had been depth. No walls, no fleet, no army But a thousand kilometers of tunnels, and a capital no raider ever found because it had no outside.
The histories his tutors taught said the Ghai had faded, collapsed, dispersed, were conquered. Something. He didn't remember.
But he did remember that their tunnels had been filled in centuries ago, sealed for safety when the palace was raised on the ruins of their mines. *Filled in.*
He remembered the phrase exactly, remembered the tutor's voice saying it, because even at ten years old he had thought: *who would fill in a thousand kilometers of tunnel? Who could?*
No one, was the answer. No one had. They had sealed the doors and written *filled in* in the books, and the books had become true because no one checked.
His machines had just checked.
He should have gone back. He knew he should have gone back. The logs alone were a life's work, the bundles in the tunnel were a hoard.
But the dark ahead of him was pulling with the specific gravity. And somewhere in that dark, faint and rhythmic in the silence he could hear his machines.
He followed the sound.

He walked for what might have been an hour, down through the labyrinth of the old kingdom, his lantern a small moving room of light in a blackness. The tunnels branched and rejoined. There were rooms, and halls.

The Ghai had cut stairs where the veins dipped, and wide hallways where the veins widened, and here and there his light brushed the ruins of their life, a rusted sled of a design he had never seen, a stack of clay lamps furred with mineral bloom, a wall of tally marks in ordered columns, thousands of them, some accounting kept by hands four hundred years dead.

The sound of the machines came and went with the turnings, closer and farther and closer and Burgundy contemplated what could happen if he got lost down here. But still he followed the sound, and soon he heard a low irregular murmur, almost like water, almost like…
Voices.
He came around a final turn and the tunnel opened, and he stopped at the edge of a space so large his lantern could not propose a shape for it.
His eyes adjusted, and the dark assembled into a cavern the size of the palace Kings' Hall three times over. But this wasn't Ghai ruin.

He saw newer timber shoring, rail lines, ore carts,, a cage elevator hanging in a shaft of work-light that fell from somewhere far above. Broken tools against the walls. Coils of cable. The living infrastructure of a working mine, grafted onto the bones of the dead kingdom.
He knew where he was. He had been here, this exact deep place, once, at twelve years old, half an hour down in the cage at his father's side, in an embroidered coat.
South 12 Shaft.
And there, across the cavern floor, in the pooled glow of the work-lights, were his machines.
The three DREKKOs had arranged themselves against a broad dark face of corvite, a monster vein, the kind the southern crews called a widow-maker, and they were working it. Calmly. Perfectly.

The nearest one placed a micro-charge with a motion as small as a nod; the crack of it was polite, almost apologetic; a sheet of ore sagged free and the second machine, blinking one red in between two green to indicate it was out of explosives, had given itself the duty of receiving the falling load its partner just cut free of the face. It was crushing, grading, pressing.

Their green panels pulsed in the dark like three calm hearts. They had come out of the palace's foundations, through a dead kingdom, into a live mine, and finding rock, finding ore, finding the thing they had taught themselves to want, they had simply gone back to work.
And in a rough half-circle around them, at the respectful, ready distance stood the miners.
Fifteen of them, maybe more at the edges of the light. Night shift, southern crew, soot-dark faces, picks still in their hands, one man holding a pry bar across his chest like a rifle at parade.

Nobody was working. Nobody was speaking anymore; whatever murmur he had heard had died when the lamplight came around the turning. They had been watching the machines. He could read it in their bodies, the awe and the fear locked together, men watching a shift's tonnage come off a widow-maker vein in perfect silence. And now, one by one, they turned, and they were watching him.

chapters.title: South 12
paragraphs: Nobody moved.

But The machines kept working. Their sound a calm hum and clank against the stillness.  The cavern held maybe twenty people now, counting the ones drifting in from the far galleries, every one of them frozen in the pooled work-light, and behind them the three Drekkos went on. A micro-charge cracked, polite as a knuckle. A sheet of ore sagged into waiting arms. The green panels pulsed their slow patient rhythm, and the sound of the work went up into the black.
Burgundy stood at the mouth of the tunnel  holding a lamp, in a princely coat he had forgotten to take off. a coat worth more than any three men in front of him earned in a year,
It was not him and it was not the woman at the front.
It was the smallest in the group.

A kid slipped out of the crowd's edge — a girl, he saw as she crossed the light, and she walked past Burgundy as if he weren't there. and in the light Burgundy could see she had one milky eye. She did not stop at the respectful distance the adults were keeping. She walked right up beside the nearest Drekko, close enough that the crack of the next charge stirred her hair, and she stood there with her face tipped up, her one eye catching the lamplight and she watched the machine work with visible fascination
"It doesn't get tired," she said.

She said it low, almost to herself, but the cavern was so quiet that it carried, and Burgundy heard in it the thing he had not been able to say to his father, to his mother, to anyone, the whole point of years of nights, spoken in four words by a child in the dark.
Then a murmur started somewhere in the crowd, and it was not about the machines.

He caught it in pieces. A man near the carts leaning to another, the second man's face changing, the word passing along the line of them the way fire passes along a fuse. He knew the word before it reached the front.
*Prince.*

And he watched what the word did, and it was not what the word did in the palace. There, it bent people at the waist. Here it moved through the crowd like cold water, awe curdling into something with more fear in it. A woman stepped back into shadow. The man with the pry bar shifted his grip, not raising it, just knowing where it was. Someone whispered something Burgundy couldn't hear, and someone else answered, low and bitter, and he caught only a piece of it — *first the sheds, now this* — and he did not need the rest. He had been at the table when the ministers reported on the shed raids. Six men taken in the night, and the taking kept quiet.

They thought he was the crackdown. Of course they did. A prince does not come down a shaft at night to admire the rock. He stood there in his coat, in the light, at the mouth of an ancient tunnel, and he watched fifteen hard-handed people arrive together at the reasonable conclusion that he had come to hang them.
Words were not going to fix it.
He turned to the machines.
"Halt," he said.
The three Drekkos stopped.

Not wound down. *Stopped* — drills stilling mid-rotation, arms freezing mid-reach, all motion cut off between one heartbeat and the next, and the silence that followed was a silence the South 12 shaft had never once held in living memory. No drill. No pick. No cough, no cage, no cart. Even the ventilation seemed to hesitate. Twenty people stood in the first true quiet of their working lives and heard, far above, water dripping somewhere in four hundred years of dark.
Every face came back to Burgundy.
It was clear now that these were his. These robots doing their work. Who obeyed his order

The woman at the front turned her head — the first time she had taken her eyes off him since the lamplight found the cavern — and looked at the crowd, and the crowd arranged itself around her look. That was all it took. No gesture, no word. Men who had been edging toward the cage drifted back.  Burgundy watched it happen and understood that he was looking at the actual authority in this cavern.
"Back to positions," the woman said. Her voice was low and carried anyway. "The quota."

They went. Not quickly, not slowly, the unhurried obedience of people who trusted the person doing the sending. In a minute the cavern had rearranged itself into something resembling a shift, picks ringing halfheartedly against rock faces nobody was looking at, and the woman crossed the floor to Burgundy with a broad russet-haired man falling in beside her, and the girl with the milk-glass eye had vanished on a cart. And now here he was, an arms length away to two miners, people he had thought about for years, but never actaully approached until this moment.
the woman did not bow and did not give her name.
"Not here," is all she said. "Whatever this is, it doesn't happen standing in the open." She tipped her head toward the tunnel mouth, toward his lamp, and started walking,

They stopped just inside the tunnel he had just come from where the work-light of the cavern fell off. The big man planted himself where he could see both the tunnel and the shaft floor at once, and Burgundy noticed that his eyes were not on Burgundy at all. They were on the halted machines, moving over them joint by joint, mount by mount, with the frank appraisal of a man who had spent his life reading load, pricing what the arms could lift.

This woman had made the a quick assessment that this wasn’t the crackdown. Maybe is was the look on Burgundy's face petrified and fearful himself. Either way her tone wasn’t not fearful. It was almost annoyed.

"You have until I say," the woman said. "Inspectors could be here any moment. They ride that cage without notice. Foremen walk this level twice a shift when they're lazy and four times when they're not. And that is a death sentence. For every person on this shift. So. Fast and straight." Her eyes went over him once, coat to boots. "Who are you. What are these. What do you want."
He gave her the truth. Most of it.

His name, which she knew. That he had built the machines, himself, alone, over two years, at night. That he had brought one to his father and his father had kicked it and forbidden him to build another. That he had secretly built three. That no one in the palace knew the machines existed. He heard himself shaping it as he went, making conscious decisions on what to leave out: his mother, the white room, the cartel channels that fed it, and some cold new part of him, some part that had learned more at council than just tribute math, noted that he was doing it smoothly. That the leaving-out did not show.
"And down here," the woman said. "How does the king's son end up standing in my shaft at midnight."

"The machines dug through." He gestured up the tunnel behind him. "I left them working against a practice wall under the palace. When I came back they'd gone through it. All the way through it and into some old tunnel, many tunnels, there's a whole network of –
"We know about the tunnels" she interjected almost rolling her eyes." Burgundy continued,
"They kept going until they found this seam. I followed them."
"You followed them."
"Yes."
"Your machines dug from the palace to South 12. On their own. Because they wanted a better seam."
"Yes."
She looked at him for a long moment, and Burgundy watched her not believe a single word of it.

He couldn't even resent it. Standing there in the lamplight, he made himself see the story from inside her life: a woman who had swung a pick for forty years, who had never touched a processor or seen a disc, being told by the tyrant's son that a machine could want, could choose, could teach itself to be a better miner four hundred times a second in the dark with nobody watching. It was absurd. He would not have believed it either. He barely believed it himself. There was no shape in her world for the true story to fit, and so she was doing the sensible thing, the survivor's thing, filing the story under *lie* and moving on to the questions that mattered.
And her questions were good. That was the thing that began, to reorganize his understanding of who he was talking to.
"Right now. Who knows the prince is not in his bed, and when do they start looking."
"No one knows. My hours are my own a night."

"Supply." She flicked two fingers at the machines. "Those aren't made of palace silverware. Tech like that comes through the cargo field or it doesn't come at all, and everything through the cargo field is weighed twice and written down. So either you're lying about no one knowing, or someone with reach is holding a door open for you and you're lying about being alone. Which."
He hesitated a half-second too long, and saw her log the hesitation like a tally mark.
"I" he hesitated again. "I have a supplier."
She brushed off the answer like he hadn't given it. There was no valuable information coming out of this conversation for her. Just threat.

"So the only question I have left" She said  "is how you leave. Quietly, tonight, forever. Just you being here for one minute is a death sentence for all of us the moment someone finds out about your science experiement.

Burgundy opened his mouth and closed it. He thought about her questions. Who audits your absence. Who supplies you. What is our exposure when your operation fails. They were not a crew chief's questions. This was a person who had run something. something with risk. with cost. with fear. something that had needed to survive being looked for by men withh guns. He stood in the tunnel. with nothing to say.
That was when the miner came.

Boots on the shaft floor, hurrying, a stocky man skidding to a stop at the tunnel mouth, wide-eyed, breathing hard. The woman's face remained tense and the arriving miner made her breathe out hard, annoyed,
"What is it."
"Hesta — the quota. The quota's in."
So her name was Hesta.
"The quota's not in," Hesta said flatly. "We're two hours into a ten-hour shift."
"I weighed it twice." The man pointed, arm not quite steady, back across the cavern floor.

The mineral carts stood in their train by the cage — full. Not heaped, not thrown; *packed*, the ore fitted and settled like masonry, and even from this distance Burgundy could see: waste rock separated out entirely, the corvite graded coarse to fine, cart by cart, better sorted sitting in the train than most loads arrived at the distribution center after a full day's handling above. The machines had done it before he ever walked into the cavern — the whole quota, ten hours of thirty miners' lungs and shoulders, pulled, sorted, graded, and packed by three machines in less time than a council session.
The crew had stopped pretending to work. They stood among the carts, touching the packed ore.

Hesta looked at the carts for a long moment. Burgundy watched her face and saw the amazement arrive and saw what it turned into — not wonder. The opposite. Her jaw set, and when she turned back to him, her eyes had gone harder than at any point since the lamplight found her.

Too good. He could read it off her like a log stream. Forty years in the shafts, fifty years on this planet, and nothing in either had ever once been this good without a hook in it. The quota in two hours was not a miracle to her. It was bait sitting in a snare she couldn't see yet, and the fact that she couldn't see it only proved how big the snare must be.

The brown-haird man who was seemingly her number 2 had no such trouble. He was looking at the carts, and then at the machines, and then at the carts, and something was kindling in his broad open face that he did not try to hide.

"Hesta." His voice was low and it shook slightly. "Do you see it? Quota by midnight. We've never done that. This could mean no more short-stipend months. No more sending the small ones into the pinch seams." He looked at the girl-shaped shadow at the edge of the cart-light, then back, and his voice dropped further, into a more serious register  "This could change everything."
"Tobin."
"I'm only saying—"

"I know what you're saying Tobin." Hesta did not raise her voice. She said it to Tobin but she kept her eyes on Burgundy, and what she said next she said slowly, so that everyone in earshot got every word. "You're standing in front of the son of the man who takes our wages, works our children, hangs our organizers. His father's men have six of ours in some dark cell right now." A pause, one beat, surgical. "And his boy came down our shaft in the night with machines we don't understand, and the first thing that happened is our quota got filled. If a fish saw a worm do that, even the fish would think twice."
Nobody laughed. It was not a joke.

Burgundy stood in the work-light with the truth in his chest — *I am not him, I built these against him* — and did not say any of it, because he understood, with a clarity that felt like Hesta's own eyes turned back on himself, that the words were worth nothing here.  Every word he could offer, an informer could offer. Every promise he could make, the regime had made and broken to these people in some generation or another. There was no sentence that proved anything.
So he said the only thing that was both true and useful.
"Tell me what you need me to do right now, and I'll do it."
Hesta studied him a moment longer. Then she made her decision the way he would learn she made all of them: completely, instantly, and with the door left open exactly one crack.

"Get these machines out of my shaft.." she said. "Now, before a foreman walks over or that cage comes down, and take half their harvest with you, I'm going to have to deal with what this looks like" to which the number 2, Tobin, gave her an incredulous look.

She stepped closer, and lowered her voice to the width of the three of them. "I'll hear you out. Once. Properly. Not here — this is a working site and I don't spend my people's necks on conversation. The full moon is three nights out, that's when the inspectors drink. Be at the bottom of your tunnel when the night shift bell rings, and wait."

She held his eyes. "You come alone. no robots.  You tell no one — and before you answer, understand that I'll know if you lie, because it's my business to know, and it has been since before you were born. Three nights."

She turned and walked back toward the carts, already calling the shift back to the pretense of work, already solving the next problem, what a full quota at hour two does to a foreman's suspicions,  and Burgundy stood at the mouth of Ghai tunnel that led him here, understanding that he had just been dismissed, scheduled, and put under surveillance in the space of a single minute, by a woman the ledgers upstairs listed as a line item.
Tobin lingered one moment longer. He put out a hand, Burgundy shook it, and his own hand vanished inside it — and the big man leaned in, and there was nothing guarded in his face at all.
"Full moon. Midnight." Tobin said. "Don't be late. And don't mind Hesta." A grin cracked through, quick and gone.
Then somewhere far above them, metal struck metal.

One clank. Then the cavern was back to work, for real this time.  Burgundy had never seen anything like it: thirty people turning toward the wall picks finding rock,  the girl with the milk-glass eye materializing atop a cart with her eyes on the cage shaft, Tobin already ten feet away with his hands full of timber. For three seconds the entire cavern was a snapshot of an ordinary shift, held taut. Obeying.

He gathered the Drekkos with a touch of the pin and started up the long dark , the three of them rolling behind him in their patient rocking gait each carrying several bundles of freshly sorted corvite.

The walk back through the dead kingdom took its hour (mostly because the Drekkos could only move so quickly), and as he went time the tunnels did not feel empty to him. He passed the tally walls and the clay lamps and the stairs worn into bowls, his lamp swinging its small room of light along the old stone, and the whole silent labyrinth felt different than it had on the way down — not abandoned.

He had stopped counting the hours without sleep somewhere on the platform at the tribute field, a day and a lifetime ago; He wound his way up through the breach, through prison cells where the logs still streamed their impossible curve, where the robots parked at their charging stations.

Then through his mother's library, the lamps out, the tens of thousands of spines asleep in the dark, the yellow book closed on its secret, down the long corridor, up to his own rooms. He washed. He lay down.
And he could not sleep.

He lay in the dark with his heart going like a drill at speed, and it was not the exhaustion and it was not the fear, though the fear was there: a foreman, a cage, a word in the wrong ear, any of a hundred threads that could end everyone in that cavern. It was the other thing. The thing with no shape in his world until tonight, the way the machines had no shape in Hesta's. Or how "real world industrial application scenarios" had no shape in the minds of the core world researchers who had given him the final ingredients to his puzzle. But tonight, theory became application. Foggy ideas became real.
Three nights. A full moon. A place he would be taken to.

He had gone down a tunnel to retrieve three runaway mining machines, and had come back up as something else — measured by a woman who ran something, scheduled into a network that had survived being looked for, four words of a child's observation still ringing in his ears. *It doesn't get tired.* His project had become something he could never have planned, never have designed, never have predicted from any log.
It had found other people.
He fell asleep as the window warmed with dawn, and he did not dream of machines. He did not dream of anything.

chapters.title: The Hollow (WIP)
paragraphs: WIP WIP WIP WIPWIP WIP
The three days in between were the strangest of his life, because nothing happened in them.

He slept most of the first one. It was a rest-day, and for once he kept it, fourteen hours down, waking in the late afternoon with the light coming copper through the curtains and his body aching in the particular way of debt being partially repaid. He ate. He slept again. Somewhere in the palace his father reviewed ledgers and his mother read in her wing and six men sat in a dark he tried not to furnish with details, and Burgundy slept like a machine with its panel gone dim.
At breakfast on the second day his mother watched him over her book.
"You slept," she said.
"I did."
"Two days."
"It caught up with me."

She turned a page. He ate. The book, he noticed, was one he had seen her reading a month ago, and her eyes were not moving along the lines. He kept eating. Eighteen months of council had taught him how to be looked at without changing shape, and he spent the whole meal being looked at, and gave her nothing, and could not tell — this was the part that stayed with him afterward — whether nothing was what she received.
On the third day he walked the grounds.

He had walked them his whole life. The palace lawns ran green and level to the southern wall — real green, watered green, the only irrigated ground within a hundred kilometers — and past the wall the land fell away in long tawny ridges toward the city, and the city climbed the far hills the way rust climbs a hull. He had seen the view ten thousand times. The workers' quarters were a texture from up here: roofs of lapped scrap going brown and orange in the afternoon light, ridge after ridge of them, woodsmoke standing up in thin grey threads, the whole thing shimmering faintly in the heat like something not quite settled.
He stood at the wall for a long time.

He had used to see it the way you see weather. Now he stood with his hands on the warm stone and found he could not stop doing arithmetic on it — how many roofs, how many under each roof, how many of the thin grey threads of smoke were cooking how little — and somewhere under one of those roofs a stocky man had weighed a train of carts twice because he could not believe the number, and somewhere a girl with a milk-glass eye was running someone's signals through streets he had never walked, and the view would not go back to being weather no matter how long he stood there.
Three nights, she had said.
He was at the bottom of his tunnel when the night bell rang.

They came for him out of the dark — two lamps swinging up the old gallery, Hesta's walk and Tobin's bulk resolving out of the black — and neither of them said more than a word. He fell in between them. They went down.

Below the working levels the party grew. At a junction where three Ghai ways met, four more figures waited in a pool of lamplight, and Burgundy's eyes went over them — a hard-faced man his father's age; a dry, upright woman older than that; a slight man who stood very still with his hands folded in front of him; and the girl, the milk-glass girl, perched on a fallen lintel with her heels drumming soft against the stone. Nobody was introduced. Hesta said only, "He's the one," which settled some question the four of them had evidently been holding, and then she turned to the oldest of them, the upright woman — no. Not her. To a figure Burgundy had missed entirely, sitting so still against the tunnel wall that she had read as stone: an old woman, small, wrapped in a miner's coat gone soft with age, with a coil of unlit lanterns strung over one shoulder like a fisherman's catch.
"Maren," Hesta said. "Take us down."
The old woman rose — not slowly, the way he expected, but all at once, the way a habit rises — and took the lead lamp, and walked into a tunnel Burgundy had not even seen was there.

The descent took the better part of an hour and he understood within the first ten minutes that no map he could ever draw would hold it. Maren did not hesitate at a single turning. She went down stairs worn to bowls and along galleries where the air moved strangely and past openings she ignored with a flatness that was itself information — that way is water, that way is the air that kills, this way is mine. Twice she said a word to the dark in a language Burgundy did not know, at places where the tunnel forked; it took him until the second time to understand she was not speaking to anyone. She was counting. Old words, worn like the stairs, a counting song gone so deep into her that it surfaced only at the turnings — and Burgundy, walking behind her through the bones of the dead kingdom, felt the hair stand up along his arms, because the song was older than the palace above them and it still worked.
Then the tunnel opened, and Maren stopped, and lit the first lantern.

He could not see the room. That was the first thing — the lamplight simply went up and did not come back. He had a sense of vastness the way you have a sense of the sea at night, by what the sound did, and the sound did something he had never heard: it left, and returned late, and returned changed.

Maren hung the first lantern in a bracket at the level of her shoulder — an ancient thing, iron gone the color of the rock, set into the wall as if grown there — and moved along the curve of the wall to the next bracket, and lit and hung the second, and by the third the others had spread out along the walls with lanterns from her coil, and Burgundy stood in the center of a darkness that was assembling itself into a room.
The light climbed in rings.

The brackets ran around the chamber at three heights — a ring at shoulder height, a ring above reach where Wraven went up the rough wall like something that had never considered falling, a third higher still, reached by ledges cut four hundred years ago for exactly this purpose — and as the lanterns filled them, ring above ring, the Hollow came out of the dark the way dawn comes: first the columns, great trunks of living rock left standing when the chamber was carved, and in the columns, veins. Corvite, threnite, ores he had no name for — five distinct veins, he would realize, once his eye learned to read them — running up through the stone like dark rivers through a pale country, converging as they climbed, all five of them meeting far overhead at the center of the vaulted ceiling in a knot of mineral the highest lanterns could just barely find. The Ghai had not chosen this chamber. They had found the place where the planet's five veins crossed, and carved the chamber around the crossing, and hung their lights beneath it.

"They brought their dead here," Maren said. It was the first full sentence she had spoken. She said it the way you name a room in your own house. "Lanterns for each one. The light was the prayer." She hung her last lantern — she had lit the first and now she lit the last, and Burgundy would learn that this was always so — and looked up once at the knot of veins in the ceiling, and then went and sat down at the table.
The table.

It stood in the center of the chamber and it should not have existed: a long heavy table of true wood, dark with age and hands, benches down both sides — carried down here, he could not begin to imagine when or how, plank by plank through an hour of labyrinth. It was not a relic. There was wax pooled in its knots and scars of use on its surface and a cleanliness that meant care. People met here. Had met here for longer than tonight. For what, he did not yet know, and looking at the seven of them settling onto the benches in the lantern light, he understood that not knowing was the point of everything that had been done to him since the night bell — he had been brought blind down an unmappable road to a room that could not be surveilled, watched the whole way by people who had made this walk more times than they would ever tell him.
The first surveillance-free room on Dross. He didn't have the thought in words yet. He would, on the walk back.
"Sit," Hesta said.
He sat.

"I'll say this part first so it's said." She did not raise her voice; the room did strange generous things with it anyway. "This meeting is costing my whole crew. They're up there right now working a true shift to cover the five of us, and every one of them had to hear from me personally about what happens if a word about your machines walks. I spent three days spending trust I've saved for twenty years." Her eyes were flat on him. "So. This had better be good."

Burgundy had prepared for this. He had spent three days preparing, walking the lawns, arranging sentences. He took a breath and gave them the speech, and the speech was earnest, and it was true, and it was — he heard it happening, the way you hear yourself in an echoing room — young.

"I want to help you. That's — I know how it sounds, but it's been the truth my whole life. I hate what my father is. The prince you see at the rim, at the festivals — that's a coat I wear so he doesn't look at what I do at night. What I am is a builder. It's the only thing I've ever been. And what I want to build —" he had his hands open on the table, he noticed, like a man showing he holds no cards — "is things that help the people in the mines."
Silence.
Then Hesta laughed.
It was not a cruel laugh. That was the worst part. It was short and low and genuinely amused, the laugh of a woman hearing an old joke told sincerely by someone too young to know it was old.

"'Help the people in the mines,'" she repeated, and let the words sit in the lantern light where everyone could look at them. "Tell me something, builder. When you say it — *the people in the mines* — what do you see?" She didn't wait. "I'll tell you what you see. You see tired backs. You see bad air and short stipends and small ones sent into pinch seams, and your chest hurts about it, honestly hurts, I'll grant you that — and you think: the problem is the work is too hard. And you're a builder, and hard work is a problem builders can solve." She leaned forward slightly. "You don't know who's at this table. You don't know what the mines *are*. You think they're a place where people work. So before you help anyone, boy, you're going to sit there and learn what it is you're offering to help."
She straightened.
"Introductions," she said, "the long way."

"Tobin you've met." She tipped her head at the big man, who was leaning back with his arms folded, entirely at ease, as if the table were his and everyone at it a guest — which, Burgundy would learn, was simply how Tobin sat everywhere. "Three generations of him are poured into South Twelfth. His grandfather's timber is still holding up half of level six; his father's is holding the rest. He knows every soul in the southern complex and what they can carry." A beat. "You'll have noticed the ear. Don't ask. Thirty years I've known him. I don't ask."
Tobin grinned at the table in general and touched the notched ear with one blunt finger, and offered nothing, and the offering of nothing was somehow warm.
"Skorn."

The hard-faced man did not nod. He had not stopped looking at Burgundy since the junction — a level, unhurried looking, the way you watch a gauge you expect to fail — and now, without a word, he reached inside his coat and brought out a book and set it on the table and pushed it the length of two places until it stopped in front of the prince.

It was small, and it was old, and it had been made by hand: boards of thin timber, a spine of cord, the whole of it worn to the softness of things carried against bodies for decades. Burgundy looked at Skorn, and Skorn looked back and said nothing, and Hesta said nothing, and the whole table let the silence instruct him. He opened it.
Names.
